pṛthivītvābhāvasya na pratyakṣatā/ maṇikārāstu yogyā
cāsāvanupalabdhiśca yogyānupalabdhiriti karmandhārayamabhipretya
pratiyogisattvaprasañjanaprasañjitapratiyogikatvaṃ yogyatvamiti
pariṣkāraṃ cakruḥ/ dīpikādau
children.translated_text: Moreover, in all the ancient treatises, taking <s>yogyānupalabdhi</s> (non-apprehension of what is fit to be apprehended) as a genitive <s>tatpuruṣa</s> compound, the expression <s>yogyānupalabdhi</s> was used to mean the absence of apprehension whose counter-positive is qualified by fitness and whose locus is qualified by fitness. Due to the qualification of 'having a fit counter-positive,' there is no perceptibility of the absence of a demon in a pillar. Due to the inclusion of 'having a fit locus as qualificand,' there is no perceptibility of the absence of earth-ness in a water-atom. But the <s>Maṇikāras</s> (authors of the <s>Tattvacintāmaṇi</s> tradition), taking [the compound] as a <s>karmadhāraya</s> — that which is both fit and a non-apprehension — refined [the definition by saying that] fitness means the property of having the existence of the counter-positive as entailed. In the <s>Dīpikā</s> and other [texts],

children.text:
maṇikṛnmatānusāreṇaiva nirvacanaṃ kṛtam/ prācīnamate 'pi na
kācidastyanupapattiriti dinakarīvyākhyāyāṃ rāmarudryāṃ spaṣṭam/
children.translated_text: the explanation has been given following the view of the <s>Maṇikāras</s> alone. That even on the ancient view there is no difficulty whatsoever is clear in the <s>Dinakarī</s> commentary [called] <s>Rāmarudrī</s>.

children.text: vyāptivicāraḥ
children.translated_text: Investigation of <s>Vyāpti</s> (Pervasion)

children.text:
tattvacintāmaṇau
anumānakhaṇḍe prācīnoktāni bahūni vyāptilakṣaṇāni anūdya dūṣayitvā
svayaṃ nirdeṣāṇyanekāni vyāptilakṣaṇāni gaṅgeśopādhyāyāḥ
pradarśayāmāsuḥ/ tatra
pratiyogyasamānādhikaraṇayatsamānādhikaraṇātyantābhāvapratiyogitāvacchedakāvacchinnaṃ
yanna bhavati tena samaṃ tasya sāmānādhikaraṇyamiti prāthamikī
siddhāntavyāptiḥ/ iyameva dīpikāyāṃ prakāśikāyāṃ ca anūditā/
taddhaṭakadalānāṃ prayojanāni ca vivecitāni/
children.translated_text: In the <s>Tattvacintāmaṇi</s>, in the section on inference (<s>anumānakhaṇḍa</s>), <s>Gaṅgeśa Upādhyāya</s>, having cited and refuted the many definitions of <s>vyāpti</s> (pervasion) stated by the ancients, presented several definitions of <s>vyāpti</s> of his own. There, the primary definition of <s>vyāpti</s> in the <s>siddhānta</s> (established conclusion) is: that which is delimited by the <s>pratiyogitāvacchedaka</s> (the delimiter of counter-positiveness) of an absolute absence that is co-located with what is co-located with that which is not co-located with the counter-positive — its co-location with that is <s>vyāpti</s>. This very [definition] has been cited in the <s>Dīpikā</s> and the <s>Prakāśikā</s>, and the purposes of its components have been analyzed.

children.text:
atredaṃ vicāryate ---
sarveṣvapi maṇikārapradarśiteṣu vyāptilakṣaṇeṣu sādhyahetvoḥ
sāmānādhikaraṇyasya praveśāt vyadhikaraṇasādhyasādhanayorapi
vyāpteriṣṭatvāt tatra kathaṃ samanvayaḥ/ tathāhi - adhodeśe
nadīpūrtyā ūrdhvadeśe vṛṣṭiranumīyate, padmasya vikāsena
sūryasyodayo 'numīyate, samudrasya vṛddhyā candrasyodayanumīyate/
tathā bhūmiṣṭhenālokena upariṣṭhaḥ savitā, cakrasya bhramaṇena bhrāmakasya
kulālasya saṃnihitatvam, kṛttikodayena rohiṇyudayāsattiḥ
ūrdhvabhāgasthadhūmenādhobhāgasthavahniścānumīyate/ etādṛśasthaleṣu
sāmānādhikaraṇyagarbhavyāpterabhāvāt
children.translated_text: Here the following is examined: since in all the definitions of <s>vyāpti</s> presented by the <s>Maṇikāra</s>, co-location (<s>sāmānādhikaraṇya</s>) of the <s>sādhya</s> (probandum) and <s>hetu</s> (probans) is incorporated, and since <s>vyāpti</s> is desired even between a <s>sādhya</s> and <s>sādhana</s> that exist in different loci — how is reconciliation [possible]? For instance: from the flooding of a river in a lower region, rainfall in an upper region is inferred; from the blooming of a lotus, the rising of the sun is inferred; from the swelling of the ocean, the rising of the moon is inferred. Likewise, from light on the ground, the sun above [is inferred]; from the rotation of a wheel, the proximity of the potter who turns it [is inferred]; from the rising of <s>Kṛttikā</s> [constellation], the nearness of the rising of <s>Rohiṇī</s> [is inferred]; and from smoke in an upper region, fire in a lower region is inferred. In such cases, since <s>vyāpti</s> embodying co-location is absent,

children.text: lakṣaṇāvyāptiḥ iti/
children.translated_text: the definition would be too narrow (<s>lakṣaṇāvyāpti</s>).

children.text:
idamatra samādhānam
--- vyadhikaraṇatayā udāhṛtasthaleṣvapi nadī vṛṣṭimadūrdhvadeśasaṃbaddhā
pūravadadhodeśasaṃbaddhatvāt, ayaṃ kālaḥ sūryodayavān
padmavikāsavatkālatvāt, ayaṃ pradeśaḥ kulālāsattimān
bhramaccakrādhikaraṇatvāt ityādyanumānānāṃ vivakṣitatvāt tatra
sāmānādhikaraṇyasyopapattiḥ/ deśataḥ vyadhikaraṇeṃṣūktasthaleṣu kālataḥ
sāmānādhikaraṇyasadbhāvāt kālikasaṃbandhasya
sādhyahetutāvacchedakatvaṃ svīkṛtya vyāptiḥ saṃpādanīyeti/
children.translated_text: Here is the resolution: even in the cases cited as instances of different-locus [inference], a river connected with an upper region possessing rainfall is flooded because of being connected with a lower region; this time possesses sunrise because of being a time possessing lotus-blooming; this region has the proximity of the potter because of being the locus of a spinning wheel — and so on. Since such inferences are what is intended, co-location is justified in those cases. In the cases cited as having spatial difference of locus, since temporal co-location obtains, <s>vyāpti</s> is to be established by accepting temporal relation (<s>kālikasaṃbandha</s>) as the delimiter of the <s>sādhya</s>-ness and <s>hetu</s>-ness.

children.text: ( 11 ) padaśaktivicāraḥ
children.translated_text: ( 11 ) Investigation of the Denotative Power of Words (<s>Padaśakti</s>)

children.text:
dīpikāyāṃ
śabdaparicchede gavādipadānāṃ gotvādijātāveva śaktiriti
mīmāṃsakamatena pūrvapakṣaṃ kṛtvā vṛddhavyavahārabalena
jātiviśiṣṭavyaktāveva śaktiriti sthāpitam/ etattattvaṃ
prācyanavyagranthavivecanapūrvakaṃ spaṣṭīkriyate/
children.translated_text: In the <s>Dīpikā</s>, in the section on verbal testimony (<s>śabdapariccheda</s>), having presented as the <s>pūrvapakṣa</s> (prima facie view) the <s>Mīmāṃsaka</s> position that the denotative power (<s>śakti</s>) of words like 'cow' etc. resides in the universal (<s>jāti</s>) such as cow-ness etc. alone, it was established that the denotative power resides in the individual (<s>vyakti</s>) as qualified by the universal, based on the conventional usage of elders (<s>vṛddhavyavahāra</s>). This truth is now clarified through an examination of both ancient and <s>Navya</s> (new) texts.

children.text:
tatrādau
nyāyasūtrakārādyāśayaḥ cintyate/ gavādiprātipadikasyārthaḥ kaḥ? kiṃ
vyaktiḥ? kiṃ vā avayavasaṃyogaviśeṣarūpā ākṛtiḥ? atha vā jātiriti
sandehaḥ/ saṃdehasya kāraṇaṃ tu avinābhāvena vartamānāsu
vyaktyākṛtijātiṣu gauriti śabdaḥ prayujyate/ tatra na jñāyate kiṃ
tāsāmanyatamaḥ śabdārthaḥ? atha vā tāḥ tisro 'pīti/ tatra vyaktivādī
āhaśabdaprayogasāmarthyāddhi padārtho niścetavyaḥ/ śabdaprayogaśyaśca
vyaktimuddiśyaiva bhavati/ tathā hi 'yā gaustiṣṭhati' 'yā gaurniṣṇā'
iti gośabdārthasya sthityādīni viśeṣaṇāni dīyante/ jāteḥ
śabdārthatve tasyāḥ ekatvāt viśeṣaṇamanupapannam,
vyāvartanīyāntarābhāvāt/ vyakteḥ padārthatve tu yā govyaktirna
tiṣṭhati tadvyāvartanārthaṃ tiṣṭhatīti viśeṣaṇaṃ saṃgacchate/ evaṃ gauḥ
upacīyate, apacīyate, gāṃ dadāti pratigṛhṇāti ityādau
vṛddhidānādikriyāsaṃbandhaḥ vyaktereva bhavati na jāteḥ/ gauḥ śuklā
kapiletyādau śuklādiguṇasaṃbandhaḥ vyakterevopapadyate/ evaṃ
gotvajāterekatvāt ekatvātiriktasaṃkhyāvattvaṃ tasyāḥ nāstīti
jāteḥ padārthatve viṃśatirgāva ityādivākyārthabodho 'nupapannaḥ/
evaṃ gosukhamityādisamāse sukhādyanvayo govyaktereva śliṣyate/
gairṅgāṃ janayatītyādau janmānvayaḥ govyakterna gotvajāteḥ/ tasmāt
vyaktireva padārtha iti/
children.translated_text: First, the intent of the <s>Nyāyasūtrakāra</s> and others is considered. What is the meaning of nominal stems like 'go' (cow) etc.? Is it the individual (<s>vyakti</s>)? Or the configuration (<s>ākṛti</s>) in the form of a particular arrangement of parts? Or the universal (<s>jāti</s>)? — such is the doubt. The cause of the doubt is that the word 'cow' is used with reference to individuals, configurations, and universals, which exist inseparably together. Among those, it is not known whether one of them is the word-meaning, or all three. There, the proponent of the individual view says: the word-meaning is to be determined from the capacity of word-usage, and word-usage occurs with reference to the individual alone. For instance, in 'the cow that stands' and 'the cow that is seated,' qualifiers such as standing etc. are given to the referent of the word 'cow.' If the universal were the word-meaning, since it is one, qualification would be unjustified, because there is nothing else to distinguish [it] from. But if the individual is the word-meaning, then the qualifier 'stands' is appropriate for distinguishing [that individual cow] from the individual cow that does not stand. Similarly, in 'the cow grows fat,' 'the cow grows thin,' 'gives a cow,' 'receives a cow,' the connection with actions of growth, giving, and the like belongs to the individual alone, not to the universal. In 'the cow is white,' 'the cow is tawny,' the connection with qualities like white etc. is justified only for the individual. Moreover, since the universal cow-ness is one, it does not possess numerality beyond one-ness; hence if the universal were the word-meaning, the comprehension of the sentence 'twenty cows' would be impossible. Similarly, in the compound 'cow-happiness' (<s>gosukha</s>) and the like, the connection with happiness etc. fits only the individual cow. In 'a cow gives birth to a cow,' the connection with birth belongs to the individual cow, not to the universal cow-ness. Therefore, the individual alone is the word-meaning.

children.text:
ākṛtivādī tu prāha
--- na vyaktiḥ padārthaḥ/ ayaṃ gauḥ ayamaśva iti prāṇināṃ yā vyavasthā
sā avayavasaṃyogarūpākṛtimapekṣya hi bhavati/ tasmāt ākṛtiḥ
padārtha iti/
children.translated_text: The proponent of the configuration view says: the individual is not the word-meaning. The classification that 'this is a cow, this is a horse' among living beings occurs with reference to the configuration in the form of a particular arrangement of parts. Therefore, the configuration is the word-meaning.

children.text:
jātivādī tu - na
vyaktiḥ nāpyākṛtiḥ padārthaḥ/ tāsāmānantyena tatra śaktigrahāsaṃbhavāt/
api ca mṛdgavake vyakterākṛteśca sadbhāve 'pi 'gāṃ prokṣaya'
'gāmānaya' ityādivākyoktaprokṣaṇānayanādikaṃ na kriyate/
vyaktivāde ākṛtivāde ca tatrāpi tatprasaṅgaḥ/ jāteḥ padārthatve tu
mṛdgavake gotvajātyabhāvāt na prokṣaṇādikamiti/
children.translated_text: The proponent of the universal view [says]: neither the individual nor the configuration is the word-meaning — because, due to their infinitude, the grasping of denotative power with respect to them is impossible. Moreover, even though the individual and the configuration exist in a clay model of a cow, the consecration, bringing, and the like enjoined in sentences such as 'consecrate the cow' and 'bring the cow' are not performed [with respect to it]. On the individual view and the configuration view, there would be the unwanted consequence [that these actions should apply] there too. But on the universal view, since the universal cow-ness is absent in a clay cow, there would be no consecration and the like.

children.text:
paraṃ tu jātipakṣe 'pi
agṛhyamāṇāyāṃ vyaktau ākṛtau ca jāteragrahāt jātijñānasya
vyaktyākṛtiviṣayakatvaniyamāt jātimātraṃ na padavācyaṃ
bhavitumarhantītyākṣepo vartate/ ataḥ kaḥ padārtha iti
children.translated_text: However, even on the universal view, an objection remains: since the universal is not grasped when the individual and the configuration are not grasped, and since the cognition of the universal necessarily has the individual and configuration as its objects, the universal alone cannot be the word-referent. Therefore, the question arises: what is the word-meaning?

children.text:
jijñāsāyāmuktaṃ
sūtrakāreṇa ---
children.translated_text: In response to this inquiry, the <s>Sūtrakāra</s> states —

children.text:
'jātyākṛtivyaktayastu
padārthaḥ' (nyā.sū. 2-2-67) iti/ asyaivaṃ vyākhyānam -- triṣvekā
śaktiriti sūcanāyapadārtha ityekavacanam/ kadācit vyakteḥ
prādhānyam, kadācidākṛteḥ kadācijjāteḥ iti prādhānyānusāreṇa
padārthatvamiti viśeṣasūcanāya tuśabdaḥ/ yadā bhedavivakṣā
vyaktiviśeṣāvagatiśca gaustiṣṭhati gaurniṣaṇṇeti tadā vyaktiḥ
padārthaḥ aṅge jātyākṛtī/ yadā tu bhedo 'vivakṣitaḥ
sāmānyāvagatiśca tadā jātiḥ padārthaḥ yathā gaurna padā
spraṣṭavyetyādau/ piṣṭakamayyo gāvaḥ kriyantāmityādau ākṛtiḥ
padārtha iti/
children.translated_text: 'The universal, configuration, and individual are the word-meaning' (<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.2.67). Its explanation is as follows: the singular 'word-meaning' indicates that the denotative power is one among the three. The word 'tu' (but) indicates the specific point that word-meaning-ness applies according to prominence — sometimes the individual is prominent, sometimes the configuration, sometimes the universal. When the intention is to distinguish and there is apprehension of a specific individual, as in 'the cow stands,' 'the cow is seated,' then the individual is the word-meaning, with the universal and configuration as subordinate. But when difference is not intended and there is a general apprehension, then the universal is the word-meaning, as in 'a cow should not be touched with the foot.' In cases like 'let cows made of flour be fashioned,' the configuration is the word-meaning.

children.text:
evamapi lāghavāt
jātāveva śaktirastu, itarayorlakṣaṇayaiva bodho bhavatu iti
śaṅkā jāyate/ atroktaṃ tātparyaṭīkāyām - gośabdaśravaṇānantaraṃ
viditasaṃgateḥ puruṣasya ekakāle vyaktyākṛtijātīnāṃ bodho
bhavati, na punaryathā 'gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ prativasati' ityatra vā
'gaurvāhīkaḥ' ityatra vā gaṅgātvagotvāvagamottaraṃ vākyārthe
tatsambandhānupapatteḥ tadavinābhāvena vā lakṣyamāṇaguṇayogena vā
tīraṃ vāhīko vāvagamyate tathehāvagatiḥ/ api tu
yugapadevāvagatiḥ/ ato 'vagatirūpeṇa kāryeṇa kalpanīyā
padaśaktistriṣu padārtheṃṣu viśrāmyati,
trayāṇāmekakāle 'vagatyāviśeṣāditi/
iyaṃ prācīnanyāyagrantharītiḥ/
children.translated_text: This is the approach of the ancient <s>Nyāya</s> texts.

Even so, the doubt arises: for the sake of parsimony, let the denotative power reside in the universal alone, and let the comprehension of the others be through secondary signification (<s>lakṣaṇā</s>). To this, the <s>Tātparyaṭīkā</s> responds: upon hearing the word 'cow,' a person who knows the convention has a simultaneous cognition of the individual, configuration, and universal at one time — and it is not the case that, as in 'The cowherd settlement dwells on the <s>Gaṅgā</s>' or in '<s>gaur</s> [means] a <s>Vāhīka</s> person,' after first cognizing <s>Gaṅgā</s>-ness or cow-ness, the bank or the <s>Vāhīka</s> is then understood through the impossibility of the relation [of the primary meaning] with the sentence-meaning or through the connection with a quality indicated by invariable association — rather, here the cognition is simultaneous. Therefore, the denotative power of a word, to be postulated on the basis of cognition as its effect, rests in all three word-meanings, since there is no difference in the simultaneous cognition of the three.

children.text: navyanaiyāyikāstu
children.translated_text: The <s>Navya-Naiyāyikas</s> (New Logicians), however,

children.text:
ghaṭādipadāt
ghaṭatvaghaṭakṛtiprakārakavyaktiviśeṣyakabodhodayāt
jātyākṛtiviśiṣṭavyaktau ghaṭādipadānāṃ śaktiḥ/
ātmādāvākṛtyabhāvāt jātiviśiṣṭavyaktau śaktiḥ/
ākāśādipadānāmupādhiviśiṣṭe śaktiḥ, ākāśajātyabhāvāt/ tatrāpi
ghaṭatvādeḥ śakyatve sati śakyatāvacchedakatvamapyaṅgīkriyate/
avayavasaṃyogaviśeṣarūpākṛteḥ śakyatve 'pi śakyatāvacchedakatvaṃ
nāṅgīkriyate, jāteriva sākṣātsaṃbandhena śakyavyaktyavṛttitvāt,
svāśrayasamavetatvarūpaparamparāsaṃbandhenaiva śakyatāvacchedakatvaṃ
vācyamiti gauravāt ityāhuḥ/
children.translated_text: since from words like 'pot' etc. there arises a cognition having pot-ness and pot-configuration as qualifiers and the particular [individual] as qualificand, the denotative power of words like 'pot' etc. resides in the individual as qualified by the universal and configuration. For things like the self (<s>ātman</s>), where configuration is absent, the denotative power resides in the individual as qualified by the universal alone. For words like 'space' (<s>ākāśa</s>) etc., the denotative power resides in what is qualified by a limiting property (<s>upādhi</s>), since there is no universal such as space-ness. Even there, the status of universals like pot-ness as delimiters of denotation (<s>śakyatāvacchedaka</s>) is also accepted. But for configuration in the form of a particular arrangement of parts, although it is part of the denotation, the status of delimiter of denotation is not accepted — because, like the universal, it does not directly inhere in the denoted individual, and it would be cumbersome to state that the delimiter of denotation operates through the indirect relation of inhering in what inheres in its own substratum — thus they say.

children.text:
anye tu
saṃsthānānupasthitāvapi gotvādinā gavādyanvayabodhāt
jātiviśiṣṭavyaktāveva gavādipadānāṃ śaktiḥ/ saṃsthāne ca pṛthageva
śaktirityāhuḥ/ paraṃ tvasmin pakṣe sūtrasthamekavacanamasvarasaṃ bhavati/
children.translated_text: Others, however, [say] that since comprehension of cow etc. occurs through cow-ness etc. even without the presentation of configuration, the denotative power of words like 'cow' etc. resides in the individual as qualified by the universal alone. And denotative power in configuration is a separate matter, they say. However, on this view, the singular number in the <s>sūtra</s> becomes discordant.

children.text: mīmāṃsakamatapariśīlanam
children.translated_text: Examination of the <s>Mīmāṃsaka</s> view

children.text:
yattu mīmāṃsakaiḥ
prathamopasthitatvājjātāveva śaktirityuktam, tadviparītam/
āśrayapratītimantarā jātiguṇayorevāpratīteḥ/ vyaktirhi prathamato
jñāyate/ tato vyaktigatavyañjakākṛtiviśeṣadarśanānantaraṃ
vyaṅgyāyāḥ jāteḥ
children.translated_text: As for the <s>Mīmāṃsakas</s>' claim that the denotative power resides in the universal alone because it is apprehended first — that is incorrect. For without the cognition of the substratum, the universal and qualities are never cognized. Indeed, the individual is cognized first. Then, upon seeing the distinctive configuration that reveals it, the cognition of the universal that is revealed [by the configuration]

children.text:
pratītirityanubhavasiddham/ kiṃ ca
saṃyuktasamavetaviṣayakacākṣuṣaṃ prati cakṣussaṃyuktasamavāyaḥ kāraṇam/
tasya ca saṃyogapūrvakatvāt dravyacākṣuṣatvāvacchinnaṃ prati
cakṣussaṃyogasya kāraṇatayā jātyādipratyayāt prāk
sāmagrīvaśājjāyamānaṃ dravyapratyakṣaṃ nāpalapituṃ
children.translated_text: follows — this is established by experience. Moreover, the visual perception directed at what inheres in what is in contact [with the sense organ] requires contact-inherence of the eye as its cause. And since that [inherence relation] is preceded by contact, the visual perception delimited by the perception of substance, having the contact of the eye as its cause, [arises first] — the perception of substance arising from the aggregate [of causal conditions] prior to the cognition of the universal and the like cannot be denied.

children.text: śakyam/

nanu ayaṃ daṇḍīti
jñānavat ayaṃ ghaṭa iti jñānamapi viśiṣṭajñānatvāt
viśeṣaṇajñānapūrvakamāstheyam/ viśeṣaṇajñānaṃ ca na
viśiṣṭārthaviṣayakam, anavasthāprasaṅgāt/ ato jātimātraviṣayakaṃ
tadityavaśyamaṅgīkaraṇīyamiti jātyādeḥ prathamopasthitatvaṃ
vaktavyamiti cet -- satyaṃ viśiṣṭajñānaṃ viśeṣaṇajñānajanyamiti/
tadeva ca viśeṣaṇajñānaṃ na jātimātraviṣayakam/
jātibhāsakasaṃnikarṣasya saṃyuktasamavāyarūpasya
tadāśrayavyaktibhāsakasaṃyogakhyasaṃnikarṣaghaṭitatayā tajjanyajñānasya
jātiviṣayakatvavat tadāśrayavyaktiviṣayakatvasyāpi durvāratvāt/ na
caivamanavasthā, viśeṣaṇajñānasya jātivyaktyubhayaviṣayakasyāpi
vaiśiṣṭyāviṣayakatayā viśiṣṭajñānatvābhāvana tatra
viśeṣaṇajñānāntarasyānapekṣaṇāt/ ato viśeṣaṇajñānakāraṇatvabalāt
jāteḥ prathamopasthitatvaṃ bhavediti pratyāśā na kāryā/
children.translated_text: Objection: 'This is a man with a staff' — cognition such as 'this is a pot' is also a <s>viśiṣṭajñāna</s> (qualified cognition), being a cognition of a qualified object, and therefore it should be accepted as preceded by a cognition of the qualifier. And the cognition of the qualifier is not one whose object is a qualified entity, for that would lead to an infinite regress. Therefore it must be accepted that it has only the <s>jāti</s> (universal) as its object, and hence it must be stated that the <s>jāti</s> and so forth are what first present themselves [to cognition]. Reply: True, a <s>viśiṣṭajñāna</s> (qualified cognition) is produced by a cognition of the qualifier. But that very cognition of the qualifier does not have merely the <s>jāti</s> (universal) as its object. For the <s>saṃnikarṣa</s> (sense-contact) that reveals the <s>jāti</s>, being of the nature of <s>saṃyuktasamavāya</s> (contact-cum-inherence), is constituted by the <s>saṃyoga</s> (contact) type of sense-contact that reveals the individual (<s>vyakti</s>) that is the substratum of that [universal]; and therefore the cognition produced by it inescapably has both the <s>jāti</s> and its substratum-individual as its objects. Nor does an infinite regress arise in this way, because the cognition of the qualifier, though having both the <s>jāti</s> and the <s>vyakti</s> as its objects, does not have the qualification-relation (<s>vaiśiṣṭya</s>) as its object, and hence is not a <s>viśiṣṭajñāna</s> (qualified cognition), so that no further cognition of a qualifier is required for it. Therefore, the expectation that the <s>jāti</s> would be what first presents itself by virtue of being the cause as a qualifier-cognition should not be entertained.

children.text:
evaṃ lāghavājjātimātre
śaktirityanupapannam/ vyaktiparaprayogasyaiva bāhulyena bahutra
vyaklikṣaṇāyāḥ kalpanīyatayā gauravāt/ tadapekṣayā viśiṣṭavyaktau
śaktiṃ svīkṛtya kvācitkajātiparaprayogasya lākṣaṇikatāyā eva
yuktatvāt/ 'vrīhibhiryajeta' ityādividhivākyeṣu sarvatra
vrīhyādipadānāṃ vyaktilākṣaṇikatve sati 'na vidhau paraḥ śabdārthaḥ'
iti nyāyavirodhaśca syāt/
children.translated_text: Similarly, the [Mīmāṃsaka] position that the denotative power resides in the <s>jāti</s> (universal) alone, by reason of simplicity, is untenable. For the usage of words referring to individuals is more prevalent, occurring in many contexts, so that positing the denotative capacity in the individual-denoting function in all those numerous cases would involve greater complexity. In comparison to that, it is more reasonable to accept that the denotative power resides in the individual qualified by the universal, and to treat the occasional usage of words with reference to the <s>jāti</s> alone as <s>lakṣaṇā</s> (secondary signification). Moreover, if in Vedic injunctive sentences like '<s>vrīhibhiryajeta</s>' ('one should sacrifice with rice'), the words like '<s>vrīhi</s>' ('rice') everywhere have only secondary signification for the individual, then there would be a conflict with the maxim '<s>na vidhau paraḥ śabdārthaḥ</s>' ('in an injunction, there is no secondary word-meaning').

children.text:
api ca śaktigrāhakeṣu
vyākaraṇādiṣu gavādipadānāṃ jātimātraśaktau na kimapi pramāṇaṃ
paśyāmaḥ/ vyaktivācakatvamupajīvya pravṛtteṣu sarūpādisūtreṣu
vyaktyākhyāyāmityanabhidhānāt jātivācakatvamupajīvya pravṛtteṣu
'jātyākhyāyāmekasmin' (pā.sū. 1-2-58) ityādisutreṣu kvacideva
jātyākhyāyāmityādinirdeśācca sarvatra
children.translated_text: Furthermore, among the means of ascertaining denotative power — grammar and the like — we see no evidence whatsoever for the position that words like '<s>go</s>' ('cow') have their denotative power directed at the <s>jāti</s> (universal) alone. For in the <s>sūtras</s> such as '<s>sarūpa</s>' and others, which are formulated presupposing the word's capacity to denote the individual, the expression '<s>vyaktyākhyāyām</s>' ('when denoting an individual') is not used [as a separate specification]; whereas in the <s>sūtras</s> like '<s>jātyākhyāyāmekasmin</s>' (<s>Pāṇini</s> 1.2.58) and others, which are formulated presupposing the capacity to denote the universal, the specification '<s>jātyākhyāyām</s>' ('when denoting a universal') is given only in certain cases. From this, it is understood that everywhere

children.text:
vyakterabhidheyatvaṃ
gamyate/ 'cādayo 'sattve' (pā.sū.1-4-57) ityādiparyudāsācca
dravyavācitvaṃ gamyate/ sādṛśyapratītimupajīvya pravartamānamupamānaṃ ca
na vyaktivācakatāmantareṇa ghaṭate/ 'gosadṛśo gavayaḥ'
ityatideśavākyagatagavayapadārthavyaktau sādṛśyagrahāddhi gavayo
gavayapadavācya iti śaktigrahaḥ/ liṅgaviśeṣanirṇayapuraskāreṇa
pravṛttaḥ kośo 'pi tadyogyavyaktivācakatvameva kalpayati/ āptavākyaṃ ca
'gāmānaya' 'na surāṃpiba' ityādikaṃ
pravṛttinivṛttyanvayipadārthagocaraṃ vyaktiśaktiṃ vyanakti/ vyavahāro 'pi
gavānayanapravṛttyādirvyaktivācakatva evopapadyate/ vākyaśeṣāṃ'pi
'yatrānyā oṣadhayo mlāyanta' ityādiḥ
modamānatvādiviśeṣaṇārhavyaktivācakatāmeva draḍhayati/ vivaraṇamapi
pākaṃ karotītyādi kriyādivyaktivācakatāpakṣasvarasam/
prasiddhapadasāṃnidhyamapi 'iha sahakāratarau madhuraṃ piko rauti'
ityādikaṃ dravyavācakatva eva saṃgatam/ ato gavādiśabdānāṃ
jātiśaktatve na kimapi pramāṇaṃ svārasikam/ bādhakāni ca bhūyāṃsi
children.translated_text: it is the individual (<s>vyakti</s>) that is denoted. And from the exclusionary rule '<s>cādayo 'sattve</s>' (<s>Pāṇini</s> 1.4.57) and similar [sūtras], the capacity to denote a substance (<s>dravya</s>) is understood. Moreover, <s>upamāna</s> (analogy), which operates by presupposing the cognition of similarity, cannot function without the capacity to denote individuals. For in the instructive sentence '<s>gosadṛśo gavayaḥ</s>' ('the <s>gavaya</s> is similar to a cow'), the comprehension of denotative power — namely, that the <s>gavaya</s> is denoted by the word '<s>gavaya</s>' — arises from grasping the similarity in the individual that is the referent of the word '<s>gavaya</s>' occurring in the statement of analogy. A lexicon (<s>kośa</s>), too, which operates with prior determination of the specific gender [of words], posits the capacity to denote only those individuals that are appropriate to that [gender]. And authoritative statements (<s>āptavākya</s>) such as 'Bring the cow' and 'Do not drink liquor', which pertain to objects that are the basis of activity and cessation, reveal the denotative power directed at individuals. Usage (<s>vyavahāra</s>) too, such as the activity of fetching cows, is explained only by the capacity to denote individuals. The complementary text (<s>vākyaśeṣa</s>) too, such as '<s>yatrānyā oṣadhayo mlāyanta</s>' ('where other plants wither'), reinforces only the capacity to denote individuals that are worthy of qualifiers like 'flourishing' and so forth. Explanatory glosses (<s>vivaraṇa</s>) too, such as 'performs cooking' and the like, are naturally aligned with the position that words denote individuals involved in actions. And contextual proximity of well-known words, such as '<s>iha sahakāratarau madhuraṃ piko rauti</s>' ('here on the mango tree, the cuckoo sings sweetly'), is consistent only with the capacity to denote substances. Therefore, there is no naturally arising evidence whatsoever for the position that words like '<s>go</s>' have their denotative power directed at the <s>jāti</s> (universal). And the numerous counter-arguments —

children.text: liṅgasaṃṅkhyānanvayādīni pūrvamevāpapāditāni/
children.translated_text: such as non-applicability of gender, number, and so forth — have already been established previously.

children.text:
kiṃ ca jātireva yadi
gavādiśabdārthaṃstarhi gotvaṃ vyaktiniṣṭhamitivat
gauvaryaktiniṣṭhetyapi prayogaḥ prasajyate/ gavādipadānāṃ
jātimātravivakṣayā prayoge tvatalādyapekṣā ca na syāt/ kiṃ ca khaṇḍo
gauḥ śuklo gauḥ ityādisāmānādhikaraṇyaṃ na ghaṭate/
khaṇḍatvāderjātāvananvayāt/ yattvatrocyate mīmāṃsakaiḥ lakṣyārthavyaktau
tadanvaya iti/ tadapi na/ kutrāpi vākye
lakṣyārthānvayiviśeṣaṇāprayogāt/ na hi gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣa ityādau
gaṅgāpadalakṣyārthatīrāsādhāraṇaṃ viśeṣaṇaṃ kenāpi vākye
prayujyate/ pratyuta gabhīrāyāṃ nadyāṃ ghoṣa ityādau śakyārthanvayyeva
viśeṣaṇaṃ prayujyate/ tasmā jjātiviśiṣṭavyaktau padānāṃ śaktirityeva
yuktam iti naiyāyikāḥ/
children.translated_text: Moreover, if the <s>jāti</s> (universal) alone were the meaning of words like '<s>go</s>' ('cow'), then just as the usage '<s>gotvaṃ vyaktiniṣṭham</s>' ('cowness resides in the individual') is [correct], the usage '<s>gaurvyaktiniṣṭhā</s>' ('the cow resides in the individual') would also follow [absurdly]. And when words like '<s>go</s>' are used with the intention of denoting only the <s>jāti</s>, there would be no need for case-suffixes like '<s>tal</s>' and so forth. Furthermore, co-referential usage (<s>sāmānādhikaraṇya</s>) such as '<s>khaṇḍo gauḥ</s>' ('the one-eared [animal] is a cow') and '<s>śuklo gauḥ</s>' ('the white [animal] is a cow') would not be possible, since attributes like 'one-eared' do not apply to the <s>jāti</s>. As for the reply given by the <s>Mīmāṃsakas</s> that the attribute applies to the individual which is the secondary referent — that too is not [valid], because nowhere in any sentence is a qualifier employed that applies exclusively to a secondary referent. For in sentences like '<s>gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ</s>' ('the cowherd settlement is on the <s>Gaṅgā</s>'), no one ever uses a qualifier that pertains exclusively to the bank, which is the secondary referent of the word '<s>gaṅgā</s>'. Rather, in sentences like '<s>gabhīrāyāṃ nadyāṃ ghoṣaḥ</s>' ('the settlement is on the deep river'), the qualifier is applied only in connection with the primary referent. Therefore, the <s>Naiyāyikas</s> hold that the denotative power of words resides in the individual qualified by the universal — this alone is correct.

children.text: prāmāṇyavicāraḥ
children.translated_text: Investigation of the Validity of Knowledge (<s>prāmāṇyavicāra</s>)

children.text:
dīpikāyāṃ
prāmāṇyasya jñaptāvutpattau ca svatastvaṃ paratastvaṃ ca nirucya
mīmāṃsakamatanirākaraṇapūrvakamubhayatra paratastvaṃ sthāpitaṃ
prāmāṇyavādaprakaraṇe/ etattattvaṃ prācyanavyagranthavimarśapūrvakamadhunā
vivriyate/
children.translated_text: In the <s>Dīpikā</s>, the <s>svatastva</s> (intrinsic nature) and <s>paratastva</s> (extrinsic nature) of <s>prāmāṇya</s> (validity) — both in its cognition (<s>jñapti</s>) and in its origination (<s>utpatti</s>) — were explained, and the extrinsic nature in both respects was established after refuting the <s>Mīmāṃsaka</s> position, in the section on the doctrine of validity. The truth of this matter is now elaborated after reviewing the texts of the old and new [Navya-Nyāya] authors.

children.text:
kasmiṃścidviṣaye jñāte
sati jāte jñāne prāmāṇyabuddhimantarā viṣaye pravṛttirna bhavatīti
jñānagataprāmāṇyajñānamapi pravṛttiheturiti vaktavyam/ na cedaṃ jñānaṃ
prameti jñānaṃ vināpi pravṛtterutpattyā vyatirekavyabhicārāt
prāmāṇyajñānasya pravṛttihetutvaṃ nāstīti vācyam/
bahuvittavyayāyāsasādhye yāgādau pravṛtteḥ prāmāṇyaniścayaṃ vinā
asaṃbhavāt/ na ca tatrāpyāvaśyakārthaniśyādeva pravṛttiriti vācyam/
yatsaṃśayaḥ yadvyatirekaniścayaśca yatpratibandhakau
tanniścayastaddheturityavaśyaṃ svīkaraṇīyam/ yathā vyāptisaṃśaye vā
vyāptivyatirekaniścaye vā satyanumitirna jāyata iti
vyāptiniścayo 'numitiṃ prati heturiti aṅgīkriyate, tathā
prāmāṇyasaṃśaye vā prāmāṇyavyatirekaniścaye vā sati pravṛttirna
jāyata iti pravṛttiṃ prati prāmāṇyaniścayaḥ kāraṇamiti sidhyati/ tathā
ca jñānapramātyaniścayaṃ vinā pravṛttyasaṃbhava iti/ na ca jñāne
prāmāṇyasaṃdehe
children.translated_text: When some object is cognized, a cognition arises; without a belief in the validity [of that cognition], there is no activity toward the object. Therefore, cognition of the validity (<s>prāmāṇya</s>) inherent in the cognition is also a cause of activity. One should not say that since activity arises even without the cognition 'this cognition is valid,' the cognition of validity is not a cause of activity, by citing the deviation in the negative concomitance. For in the case of activities like <s>yāga</s> (Vedic sacrifice) and the like, which require great expenditure of wealth and effort, it is impossible [to act] without certainty of validity. Nor should one say that even there, activity arises merely from the certainty of the object's necessity. For it must necessarily be accepted that whatever [state] whose doubt or whose certainty of absence is an obstruction to something, the certainty of that [state] is the cause of that [thing]. Just as, when there is doubt about <s>vyāpti</s> (pervasion) or certainty of the absence of <s>vyāpti</s>, inference does not arise, and therefore certainty of <s>vyāpti</s> is accepted as a cause of inference — similarly, when there is doubt about validity or certainty of the absence of validity, activity does not arise, and therefore certainty of validity is established as a cause of activity. And thus, without the certainty that a cognition is valid, activity is impossible. Nor [should it be objected] that when there is doubt about the validity of a cognition,

children.text:
satyarthasaṃdehāt
arthaniścayarūpakāraṇābhāvādeva pravṛttyabhāvopapattau pravṛttiṃ prati
prāmāṇyasaṃdehasya pratibandhakatvābhāvenoktaniyamāpravṛttyā
prāmāṇyaniścayasya pravṛttiṃ prati hetutvābhāvāt
prāmāṇyasvatastvaparatastvavicāro 'navasara iti vācyam/ yatra
jñānaviśeṣe pramātvasaṃdeho tatra niṣkampapravṛttiḥ
idamitthamevetyavadhāraṇādeva saṃpādanīyā/ taccāvadhāraṇaṃ jñānasya
pramātvaniścayaṃ vinā na saṃbhavatīti
pravṛttihetubhūtārthaniścayahetutayā prāmāṇyaniścayasya pravṛttiṃ prati
prayojakatvāt prāmāṇyaniścayo 'pi saṃpādanīyaḥ/ sa ca svataḥ parato
veti vicāro yukta eva/
children.translated_text: since there is doubt about the object [itself], and since the absence of the cause in the form of certainty about the object itself suffices to explain the absence of activity, therefore doubt about validity is not an obstruction to activity, and consequently, by the non-application of the stated principle, the certainty of validity is not a cause of activity, and hence the inquiry into whether validity is intrinsic or extrinsic is pointless — [this should not be said]. For where there is doubt about the validity of a particular cognition, unwavering activity must be produced precisely from the determination 'this is exactly so.' And such determination is not possible without certainty of the validity of the cognition. Therefore, since certainty of validity is a factor in [producing] certainty about the object, which [in turn] is a cause of activity, the certainty of validity is also relevant to activity and must be accounted for. And the inquiry whether it is <s>svataḥ</s> (intrinsic) or <s>parataḥ</s> (extrinsic) is entirely appropriate.

children.text:
tatra prāmāṇyajñaptau
svatastvaṃ paratastvaṃ ca maṇau pañcadhā niruktam/ tatra prathamaniruktimātraṃ
dīpikāyāmanūditam/ jñānaṃ yayā sāmagyā jñāyate tayaiva jñānagataṃ
pramātvamapi jñāyata iti jñānagrāhakasāmagrīgnāhyatvātmakaṃ prathamaṃ
svatastvam/ tatra
prābhākarā
children.translated_text: the <s>Prābhākaras</s>

children.text:
ḥ - ghaṭamahaṃ jānāmītyeva jñānākāraḥ/ tasya
jñānasya svayaṃprakāśatvāt jñānagrāhakamapi svayameveti tadgrāhyatvaṃ
prāmāṇyasyeti vadanti/
children.translated_text: [hold]: The form of cognition is simply 'I know the pot.' Since that cognition is self-luminous (<s>svayaṃprakāśa</s>), the apprehender of the cognition is the cognition itself. Therefore, they say, validity is that which is apprehended by it [i.e., the self-luminous cognition].

children.text: bhāṭṭāḥ
children.translated_text: The <s>Bhāṭṭas</s>

children.text:
--- jñānaṃ
jñātatayānumīyata iti jñātatāliṅgakānumitiḥ
jñānagrāhakasāmagrījanyagrahaḥ tadviṣayatvaṃ prāmāṇyasyetyācakṣate/
children.translated_text: [hold]: A cognition is inferred through the mark of 'having-been-cognized' (<s>jñātatā</s>). Thus the inference based on the indicator of <s>jñātatā</s> is the apprehension produced by the cognition-apprehending causal complex, and validity is that which is the object of that [inferential apprehension] — so they state.

children.text: murārimiśrāḥ
children.translated_text: The followers of <s>Murāri Miśra</s>

children.text:
--- 'ayaṃ ghaṭaḥ' iti jñānānantaraṃ
'ghaṭamahaṃ jñānāmi' ityanuvyavasāyo jāyate/ tena jñāne
viṣayīkriyamāṇe tadgataṃ pramātvamapi viṣayīkriyate/ tathā ca
jñānagrāhakānuvyavasāyagrāhyatvāt prāmāṇyasya
svatastvamityupavarṇayanti/ matatraye 'pi
jñānagrāhakasāmagrayāḥbhinnatve 'pi jñānagrāhakasāmagrīgrāhyatvātmakaṃ
svatastvaṃ
children.translated_text: [hold]: After the cognition 'this is a pot,' there arises the <s>anuvyavasāya</s> (post-cognitive reflective awareness) 'I know the pot.' When the cognition is objectified by that [reflective awareness], the validity inherent in it is also objectified. Thus, since the validity is apprehended by the <s>anuvyavasāya</s> which apprehends the cognition, <s>svatastva</s> (intrinsicality) [of validity] obtains — so they explain. In all three views, although the cognition-apprehending causal complexes differ, the <s>svatastva</s> defined as 'being apprehended by the cognition-apprehending causal complex'

Regarding the <s>svatastva</s> (intrinsic nature) and <s>paratastva</s> (extrinsic nature) of the cognition of validity, five different formulations have been given by scholars. Of these, only the first formulation is presented in the <s>Dīpikā</s>. The first [formulation of] <s>svatastva</s> consists in this: validity inherent in a cognition is cognized by the very same set of causal conditions (<s>sāmagrī</s>) by which the cognition itself is cognized — that is, being an object of the cognition-apprehending causal complex. Regarding this,

children.text:
sādhāraṇam/ atra
yatprāmāṇyāśraye jñāne doṣavaśādaprāmāṇyagrāhikā kācana sāmagrī tayā
tatprāmāṇyasyāgrahāt svatastvabādhaḥ syāditi aprāmāṇyagrāhaketi
sāmagrīviśeṣaṇaṃ deyam/ evamapi idaṃ jñānamaprameti jñānaniṣṭhasya
aprāmāṇyavati aprāmāṇyaprakārakatvarūpasya prāmāṇyasya
aprāmāṇyagrāhakasāmagryaivaṃ grahaṇāt
aprāmāṇyagrāhakasāmagrīgrāhyatvātmakasvatastvasya tatra bādhaḥ syāditi
tadvāraṇāya tadaprāmāṇyāgrāhaketi vaktavyam/ tasmin aprāmāṇgrāhaketi
tadarthaṃḥ/ yādṛśaprāmāṇye svatastvamiṣyate
tādṛśaprāmāṇyāśrayaviśeṣyakāprāmāṇyaprakārakajñānajanaketi yāvat/
idaṃ jñānamapremetyākārakajñānaniṣṭhaprāmāṇyagrāhakasāmagryāḥ/
idañjñānaviśeṣyakāprāmāṇyagrāhakatve 'pi prakṛtaprāmāṇyāśrayabhūtaṃ
yat idaṃ jñānamaprametyākārakaṃ jñānaṃ
tadviśeṣyakāprāmāṇyajñānājanakatvānna doṣaḥ/ naiyāyikairapi
jñānagrāhakaṃ yat idaṃ jñānaṃ pramā samarthapravṛttijanakatvāt
ityanumānaṃ tadgrāhyatvasya pramātve 'ṅgīkārāt
svatastvāpattivāraṇāya yāvajjñānagrāhakasāmagrīti yāvattvaviśeṣaṇamapi
deyam/ tacca sāmāgryāṃ na viśeṣaṇam/ sarvābhirjñānasāmagrībhirekasya
jñānasyājananena yāvatsāmagrījanyagrahāprasiddhaṃḥ/ api tu
jñānaviśeṣaṇam/ tathā ca
jñānagrāhakasāmagrījanyayāvadgrahaviṣayatvamiti phalitam/
tādṛśayāvadgrahāntargatānuvyavasāyagrāhyatvasya prāmāṇye
naiyāyikairanaṅgīkārānna doṣaḥ/ yāvattvasya ca vyāpakatvarūpatvāt
tadaprāmāṇyagrāhakatattaddharmaprakārakajñānagrāhakasāmagrījanyagrahatvavyāpakaviṣayitānirūpakatvaṃ
svatastvamiti dīdhitikārairniṣkarṣaḥ kṛtaḥ/ sa niṣkarṣaḥ
prakāśikāyāmanūditaḥ/
children.translated_text: is common [to all three]. Here, the qualification 'not apprehending invalidity' must be added to 'causal complex,' because if some causal complex, due to a defect, apprehends the invalidity of the cognition that is the locus of validity, then that complex would not apprehend the validity [of that cognition], and <s>svatastva</s> would be contradicted. Even so, in the cognition 'this cognition is not valid,' the <s>prāmāṇya</s> (validity) that resides in the cognition bearing invalidity — in the form of having invalidity as a qualifier — would be apprehended by the very causal complex that apprehends invalidity, and thus the <s>svatastva</s> defined as 'being apprehended by the invalidity-apprehending causal complex' would be contradicted there. To prevent this, one must say 'not apprehending the invalidity of that [very cognition whose validity is in question].' The meaning is: not generating a cognition having as its qualifier the invalidity whose locus is the same [cognition] as that in which the validity whose <s>svatastva</s> is being asserted resides. [This blocks the objection] regarding the causal complex that apprehends the cognition of the form 'this cognition is not valid,' since although it apprehends the invalidity of that particular cognition [as its object], it does not generate a cognition whose qualifier is the invalidity whose locus is the very cognition whose validity is the one under consideration — hence there is no fault. The <s>Naiyāyikas</s> too must add the qualification '<s>yāvat</s>' ('to the extent of') to 'cognition-apprehending causal complex,' because the inference 'this cognition is valid, since it produces successful activity' is the apprehension that is the object of the cognition-apprehending complex, and accepting that validity is apprehended by it would lead to the unwanted consequence of <s>svatastva</s>. And this [qualification] is not a qualifier of the causal complex [itself], since it is well known that not all cognition-producing causal complexes generate a single cognition, and hence apprehension produced by the totality of all causal complexes is not established. Rather, it is a qualifier of the cognition. Thus the upshot is: being the object of apprehension-up-to-the-extent-of that which is produced by the cognition-apprehending causal complex. Since the <s>Naiyāyikas</s> do not accept that being apprehended by the <s>anuvyavasāya</s> included within such 'apprehension-up-to-the-extent-of' constitutes validity, there is no fault. And since <s>yāvattva</s> ('up-to-the-extent-of-ness') has the nature of a universal property (<s>vyāpakatva</s>), the author of the <s>Dīdhiti</s> has drawn the conclusion that <s>svatastva</s> is: being the counter-correlate of the determiner-relation of that object-hood which pervades the apprehension produced by the cognition-apprehending causal complex that generates cognition having as its qualifier the properties whose invalidity-apprehending [cognition is not generated]. This conclusion is presented in the <s>Prakāśikā</s>.

children.text:
atha prāmāṇyavādasya tulanātmakadṛṣṭyā
vicāraḥ
children.translated_text: Now, an investigation of the doctrine of validity from a comparative perspective:

children.text:
pramātmakajñānagataṃ
prāmāṇyaṃ apramātmakajñānagatamaprāmāṇyaṃ ca kiṃ svataḥ uta parata ityatra
tīrthakarā vipratipadyante/ tatra prāmāṇyamaprāmāṇyaṃ cetyubhayaṃ svata
iti sāṃkhyāḥ/ ubhayaṃ parata iti vaiśeṣikādayaḥ/ aprāmāṇyaṃ parata
iti bauddhāḥ/ prāmāṇyaṃ svataḥ aprāmāṇyaṃ parata iti mīmāṃsakāḥ
vedāntinaśceti catvāraḥ pakṣāḥ/
children.translated_text: Whether <s>prāmāṇya</s> (validity) inherent in a cognition that is <s>pramā</s> (veridical) and <s>aprāmāṇya</s> (invalidity) inherent in a cognition that is <s>apramā</s> (non-veridical) are <s>svataḥ</s> (intrinsic) or <s>parataḥ</s> (extrinsic) — on this, the founders of philosophical schools disagree. Among them, the <s>Sāṃkhyas</s> hold that both validity and invalidity are intrinsic. The <s>Vaiśeṣikas</s> and others hold that both are extrinsic. The <s>Bauddhas</s> (Buddhists) hold that invalidity is extrinsic [and validity is intrinsic]. The <s>Mīmāṃsakas</s> and <s>Vedāntins</s> hold that validity is intrinsic and invalidity is extrinsic — thus there are four positions.

children.text: sāṃkhyamatam
children.translated_text: The <s>Sāṃkhya</s> view:

children.text:
jñāne
pūrvamavidyamānaṃ prāmāṇyamaprāmāṇyaṃ vā paścāt kāraṇabalādutpadyata
ityaṅgīkāre asatkāryavādo bhavediti bhītāḥ sāṃkhyāḥ
prāmāṇyamaprāmāṇyaṃ cetyubhayamapi svābhāvikamiti/
children.translated_text: The <s>Sāṃkhyas</s>, fearing that the acceptance that validity or invalidity — previously non-existent in the cognition — arises subsequently through the force of [external] causes would amount to <s>asatkāryavāda</s> (the doctrine that the effect does not pre-exist in the cause), [maintain that] both validity and invalidity are natural (<s>svābhāvika</s>).

children.text:
paraṃ tu ubhayamapi
hetuviśeṣaṃ vinā yadi svabhāvato bhavetām, tadā 'idaṃ jñānaṃ
pramāṇaṃ' 'idaṃ jñānamapramāṇam' iti vyavasthā na syāt iti
asvārasyamasmin mate 'sti/
children.translated_text: However, if both were to arise naturally, without any specific cause, then the determination 'this cognition is valid' or 'this cognition is invalid' would not be possible — this is the difficulty in this view.

children.text: bauddhamatam
children.translated_text: The <s>Bauddha</s> (Buddhist) view:

children.text:
aprāmāṇyaṃ svataḥ
prāmāṇyaṃ parata iti manyante bauddhāḥ/ tathā hi --- yadi prāmāṇyaṃ
svata eva niścīyate, tarhi prāmāṇyarūpaikatarakoṭeḥ niścayāt idaṃ
jñānaṃ pramā apramā veti saṃśayo na syāt/ ataḥ kāraṇabhūtasya guṇasaya
jñānāt pravṛttisaṃvādācca prāmāṇyaṃ niścīyate/
children.translated_text: The Buddhists hold that invalidity is intrinsic (<s>svataḥ</s>) while validity is extrinsic (<s>parataḥ</s>). For thus — if validity were ascertained intrinsically, then since one of the two alternatives, namely the nature of validity, would already be determined, there could be no doubt of the form 'Is this cognition valid (<s>pramā</s>) or invalid (<s>apramā</s>)?' Therefore, validity is ascertained from the knowledge of a quality (<s>guṇa</s>) that is the cause, and from the conformity of activity (<s>pravṛttisaṃvāda</s>).

children.text: taduktam ---
children.translated_text: As it has been said —

children.text:
'tasmin sadapi
mānatvaṃ viniścetuṃ na śakyate/
children.translated_text: 'Even when validity exists in it, it cannot be definitively ascertained;

children.text:
uttarārthakriyājñānāt
kevalaṃ tat pratīyate//'
children.translated_text: it is cognized only through subsequent knowledge of successful activity (<s>arthakriyā</s>).'

children.text:
iti/ aprāmāṇyaṃ tu
svata evāvasīyate/ ata eva vedādutpannaṃ jñānaṃ viparyayarūpam/ ataḥ
svato 'pramāṇaṃ vedāḥ iti bauddhānāmākūtam/
children.translated_text: Thus. But invalidity is ascertained intrinsically alone. Therefore, the cognition arising from the <s>Vedas</s> is of the nature of error (<s>viparyaya</s>). Hence the intent of the Buddhists is that the <s>Vedas</s> are intrinsically invalid (<s>apramāṇa</s>).

children.text:
idamatra dūṣaṇam/
aprāmāṇyaṃ svābhāvikamiti vādināṃ mate 'pi bhramajñāne 'dhiṣṭhānāṃśe
prāmāṇyasya svābhāvikatvaṃ vaktavyam/ anyathā
niradhiṣṭhānabhramaprasaṅgāt/ kiṃ ca 'pramāṇāt prameyasiddhiḥ'
'yuktiyuktaṃ vaco grāhyam' ityādikaṃ vacanaṃ sarvairapi vādibhiḥ
svataḥ pramāṇamiti vaktavyam/ tathā nirvikalpakasya
vāsanopaplavaśūnyasya svata eva prāmāṇyamupagacchanti/ savikalpakasyāpi
svāṃśe prāmāṇyaṃ viṣayāṃśe 'prāmāṇyaṃ ca vadanti/ tathā ca kutracit
prāmāṇyasvatastvaṃ teṣāmapyavarjanīyam/ api ca sarveṣvapi jñāneṣu
kiñcidaṃśe prāmāṇyasya sattvāt aprāmāṇyasyaiva kvācitkatvāt tadeva
kiṃśukādyupādhikāruṇyavat sahetukaṃ, prāmāṇyameva nirhetukamiti
vyavasthāpanāt iti mīmāṃsakāḥ/ naiyāyikāstu doṣataḥ aprāmāṇyaṃ
guṇataḥ prāmāṇyamityāhuḥ/ sarvathā aprāmāṇyasvatastvaṃ na ghaṭate/
children.translated_text: Here is the refutation: Even in the view of those who maintain that invalidity is intrinsic, in the case of erroneous cognition, the intrinsic nature of validity with respect to the substratum-aspect (<s>adhiṣṭhāna</s>) must be acknowledged. Otherwise, there would be the absurd consequence of error without any substratum. Moreover, statements such as 'from a valid means of knowledge, the object is established' and 'speech endowed with reasoning should be accepted' must be acknowledged by all disputants as intrinsically valid. Likewise, they accept that <s>nirvikalpaka</s> (indeterminate cognition), being free from the taint of latent impressions (<s>vāsanā</s>), has intrinsic validity. And they say that even <s>savikalpaka</s> (determinate cognition) has validity in its own aspect and invalidity in the object-aspect. Thus, intrinsic validity in some respect is unavoidable even for them. Moreover, since validity exists in some aspect in all cognitions, and invalidity is only occasional, invalidity alone is caused — like the redness in the Kiṃśuka tree and similar cases which is due to an adventitious condition — while validity is uncaused. Thus establish the <s>Mīmāṃsakas</s>. The <s>Naiyāyikas</s>, however, say that invalidity arises from defects (<s>doṣa</s>) and validity from excellences (<s>guṇa</s>). In any case, intrinsic invalidity is untenable.

children.text: mīmāṃsakamatam/
children.translated_text: The <s>Mīmāṃsaka</s> view:

children.text:
prāmāṇyaṃ svata
evotpadyate jñāyate ca/ aprāmāṇyaṃ tu parata utpadyate jñāyate ceti
mīmāṃsakāḥ/ prāmāṇyaṃ svata utpadyata ityasya prāmāṇyāśrayajñānasya yā
sāmagrī utpādikā tayaiva jñānagataṃ prāmāṇyamapyutpadyate, na tu
guṇādityarthaḥ/ tena ca vedādutpannasya jñānasya yat prāmāṇyaṃ tatra
vaktṛyathārthajñānarūpaguṇāpekṣāvirahāt vedasyāpauruṣeyatvaṃ sthiraṃ
bhavatīti teṣāmāśayaḥ/ prāmāṇyaṃ svato jñāyata ityasya
prāmāṇyāśrayasya jñānasya yayā sāmagryā jñānaṃ bhavati tayaiva
tadgataprāmāṇyasyāpi jñānaṃ bhavati/ paścāttu
bādhakajñānakāraṇadoṣajñānābhyāṃ prāmāṇyaṃ bādhyate/ evaṃ ca apauruṣeye
vede anāptapuruṣasaṃbandhakṛtadoṣāṇāmabhāvāt bādhakajñānābhāvācca
jñātaṃ prāmāṇyaṃ tathaivāvatiṣṭhate/ tathā ca vedaprāmāṇyasthirīkaraṇameva
jñaptau svatastvasādhanasya prayojanamiti/
children.translated_text: Validity is intrinsically produced and intrinsically cognized. Invalidity, however, is extrinsically produced and extrinsically cognized — thus say the <s>Mīmāṃsakas</s>. The meaning of 'validity is intrinsically produced' is: by the very aggregate of causal conditions (<s>sāmagrī</s>) that produces the cognition which is the locus of validity, the validity residing in that cognition is also produced — not by any excellence (<s>guṇa</s>). And thereby, regarding the validity of cognition arising from the <s>Vedas</s>, since there is no dependence on an excellence in the form of the speaker's veridical knowledge, the authorlessness (<s>apauruṣeyatva</s>) of the <s>Vedas</s> stands firm — this is their intent. The meaning of 'validity is intrinsically cognized' is: by the very aggregate of causal conditions by which the cognition that is the locus of validity comes into being, the knowledge of the validity residing in it also comes into being. Subsequently, however, validity is sublated by knowledge of a sublating cognition (<s>bādhakajñāna</s>) and by knowledge of defects in the cause. Thus, in the case of the authorless <s>Vedas</s>, since there is an absence of defects caused by connection with unreliable persons, and since there is no sublating cognition, the cognized validity remains as it is. And thus, the purpose of establishing intrinsic cognizability is precisely to secure the validity of the <s>Vedas</s>.

children.text: prāmāṇyaniścaye nyāyadarśanābhiprāyaḥ
children.translated_text: The view of <s>Nyāya</s> philosophy on the ascertainment of validity:

tattvenānavadhārayan pramājanakasya tattvamavadhārayituṃ śaknoti/
pramāyāśca tattvamavyabhicāritvarūpaṃ svataḥ parato vā

viṣayīkartumaśaknuvat kathaṃ hi nāma svagataṃ pramātvaṃ grahīṣyatīti
svataḥ pakṣaḥ tāvanna yuktaḥ/ jñānaṃ svayaṃprakāśam iti pakṣe 'pi
kathañcit jñānasya svaviṣayakatvasambhave 'pi
svagatāvyabhicāritvarūpapramātvaviṣayakatvaṃ durūpapādam/ parataḥ

vā arthakriyāviṣayakajñānasya vā anyasya vā vivakṣāyāṃ teṣāmapi
svasmin pramātvānavadhāraṇe pūrvajñāne prāmāṇyaṃ kathaṃ jñātum
śakyeta/ atasteṣāṃ prāmāṇyaṃ jñānāntarebhyaścet teṣāmapi
tathetyanavasthā/ teṣāṃ pramātvaṃ svata iti tu
pūrvoktarītyānupapannam/ tathā ca svataḥ parato vā
pramātattvānavadhāraṇāt pramāṇatattvāvadhāraṇaṃ na sambhavati/
tadasaṃbhavācca prameyāditattvajñānamapi na saṃbhavati/ tasmāt
pramāṇādiṣoḍaśapadārthatattvajñānānniḥśreyasādhigama
ityupadiśacchastramanarthakamityāśaṅkāyāḥ nirākaraṇārthaṃ"pramāṇato arthapratipattau"
ityādibhāṣyaṃ pravṛttamiti/
children.translated_text: Although in the <s>Nyāyasūtras</s> no inquiry into the intrinsic or extrinsic nature of validity and invalidity has been made, nevertheless, by the <s>sūtra</s> 'Its validity is like that of <s>mantras</s> and <s>Āyurveda</s>, and arises from the authority of reliable persons (<s>āpta</s>)' (<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.1.68), extrinsic validity is indeed indicated. The <s>Nyāyabhāṣya</s> author arranged the very opening statement as indicative of the extrinsic nature of validity — 'A valid means of knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>) is one that is productive of objects, since it has the capacity to generate purposeful activity from the apprehension of objects.' And this <s>bhāṣya</s> passage was introduced by <s>Vācaspatimiśra</s> as follows: Objection — a treatise that teaches a means impossible to practice is purposeless, like a treatise teaching how to obtain the crest-jewel from <s>Takṣaka</s> the serpent to cure fever. This <s>Nyāyaśāstra</s> too is of the same kind. For in this treatise, the highest good (<s>niḥśreyasa</s>) is taught as resulting from the true knowledge of the sixteen categories (<s>padārtha</s>). But that itself is unattainable. The true knowledge of objects such as <s>prameya</s> depends on the true knowledge of the means of valid knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>). For a means of valid knowledge, when not truly determined, is incapable of ascertaining its own object. And the ascertainment of the true nature of <s>pramāṇa</s> depends on the ascertainment of the true nature of valid cognition (<s>pramā</s>). For one who has not truly ascertained <s>pramā</s> cannot ascertain the true nature of what produces <s>pramā</s>. And the true nature of <s>pramā</s> — its unerring character (<s>avyabhicāritva</s>) — cannot be ascertained either intrinsically or extrinsically. How indeed could a cognition directed toward objects like pots, being unable to make itself its own object, grasp its own character as valid cognition? Thus the intrinsic view is first shown to be untenable. Even on the view that cognition is self-luminous (<s>svayaṃprakāśa</s>), although somehow the cognition's self-objectification may be possible, its having as its object its own unerring valid-cognition nature is difficult to establish. On the extrinsic view too, whether by 'extrinsic' one means another cognition having the first cognition as its object, or a cognition having successful activity as its object, or something else — since for those too, validity in themselves is not ascertained, how could validity in the prior cognition be known? If their validity is from further cognitions, then for those too likewise — hence infinite regress. That their validity is intrinsic is untenable in the manner already stated. Thus, since the true nature of valid cognition cannot be ascertained either intrinsically or extrinsically, the ascertainment of the true nature of <s>pramāṇa</s> is impossible. And from its impossibility, the true knowledge of <s>prameya</s> and other categories is also impossible. Therefore, the treatise that teaches the attainment of the highest good from the true knowledge of the sixteen categories including <s>pramāṇa</s> would be purposeless — to remove this doubt, the <s>bhāṣya</s> beginning with 'from the apprehension of objects through <s>pramāṇa</s>' was composed.

children.text:
asya bhāṣyasyāyamarthaḥ -
prāmāṇamarthavaditi pratijñā/ pravṛttisāmarthyāditi hetuḥ/ pramāṇamiti
karaṇārthakalyuḍantaḥ śabdaḥ/ arthavaditi nityayoge matup/ nityatā
cārthāvyabhicāritā/ arthāvyabhicāritvaṃ ca tadvati tatprakārakatvam/
tacca pramāṇasya jñānadvārakam/ tathā ca pramāṇaṃ tadvati
tatprakārakajñānajanakamiti pratijñārthaḥ/ samapravṛttijanakatvamiti
tadarthaḥ/ yadi pramāṇamarthāvyabhicāri nābhaviṣyat samarthāṃ pravṛttiṃ
nākariṣyat yathā arthavyabhicārī pramāṇābhāsa iti
vyatirekyanumānamatra
children.translated_text: The meaning of this <s>bhāṣya</s> is as follows: '<s>Pramāṇa</s> is productive of objects' — this is the thesis (<s>pratijñā</s>). 'From the capacity to generate activity' — this is the reason (<s>hetu</s>). The word '<s>pramāṇa</s>' ends in the <s>karaṇa</s>-signifying <s>lyuṭ</s> suffix. '<s>Arthavat</s>' has the <s>matup</s> suffix in the sense of constant connection. And constancy is non-deviation from the object. Non-deviation from the object is having a qualifier that corresponds to what is qualified. And this operates through cognition in the case of <s>pramāṇa</s>. Thus the meaning of the thesis is: <s>pramāṇa</s> is that which produces a cognition whose qualifier corresponds to what is qualified. 'Having the capacity to generate appropriate activity' — this is its meaning. If <s>pramāṇa</s> were not non-deviating from objects, it would not produce effective activity, just as a pseudo-means of knowledge (<s>pramāṇābhāsa</s>) which deviates from the object does not — this is the intended negative inference (<s>vyatirekyānumāna</s>).

children.text:
vivakṣitam/ pramāṇasya
pravṛttijanakatvaṃ na sākṣāt, kiṃ tu
arthapratipattijananadvāreṇetyāśayena pramāṇator'thapratipattāvityuktam/
tathā ca vipratipannaṃ jñānaṃ tadvati tatprakārakaṃ
saphalapravṛttijanakatvādityanumāna eva paryaṃvasānam/ itthaṃ ca
saphalapravṛttijanakatvahetukānumityā jñānagataṃ pramātvaṃ gṛhyata iti
bhāṣyakārāśayaḥ/
children.translated_text: The capacity of <s>pramāṇa</s> to generate activity is not direct, but rather through the medium of producing the apprehension of the object — with this intent it was said 'from the apprehension of objects through <s>pramāṇa</s>.' Thus, a cognition under dispute is one whose qualifier corresponds to what is qualified, because it generates successful activity — this ultimately rests on inference alone. In this way, the validity residing in cognition is grasped through an inference whose reason is the capacity to generate successful activity — this is the intent of the <s>bhāṣya</s> author.

children.text:
nanvanumitirūpajñānaniṣṭhaṃ pramātvaṃ kena gṛhyate?

kimarthaṃ tatra
pravṛttisāmarthyaliṅgakānumityanudhāvanamiticet--idaṃ jñānaṃ
pramā na veti saṃśayānurodhena pramātvaniścayāya

prāmāṇyasyāvaśyavedyatvānabhyupagamānnānavastheti kusumāñjalikārāḥ
upapādayanti2/
children.translated_text: Objection: By what is the validity residing in the inferential cognition itself grasped? If by another inference, then there is infinite regress — if so objected, the answer is: No. Because the <s>anuvyavasāya</s> (retrospective cognition) directed at the inferential cognition, while grasping the inference, also grasps the validity residing in it; thus the validity of the inference is accepted as intrinsically grasped. Then let the validity also be grasped by the <s>anuvyavasāya</s> 'I know the pot' when the pot-cognition is grasped — what need is there to pursue an inference with the mark of capacity to generate activity? To this the <s>Tātparyaṭīkā</s> authors explain: In response to the doubt 'Is this cognition valid or not?', for the purpose of ascertaining validity, there is recourse to the logical reason in the form of capacity to generate activity; in the present case [of <s>anuvyavasāya</s>], since that [doubt] is absent, [no such inference is needed]. The <s>Kusumāñjali</s> author establishes that there is no infinite regress because there is no acceptance that validity must necessarily be cognized.

In the <s>Kusumāñjali</s>, the extrinsic nature both in cognizability and in origination

children.text: anyathākhyātivicāraḥ
children.translated_text: Examination of <s>Anyathākhyāti</s> (the theory of error as 'apprehension of the other as otherwise'):

children.text:
bhramātmakajñānasya
khyātiriti vyapadeśaḥ śāstragrantheṣu vartate/ tatra viṣaye vādino
bahudhā vadanti/ loke yasya yasya yadyat jñānaṃ bhavati tatsarvaṃ prameti
vaktuṃ na śakyate/ tathā sati prativādino jñānamapi pramā syāt/ tathā
ca prativādyapi vijayeta/ tathāsarvaṃ jñānamaprametyapi vaktuṃ na pāryate/
tathā sati vādino yat jñānaṃ tadapyapramā syāt/
children.translated_text: In philosophical treatises, the designation '<s>khyāti</s>' is used for cognition that is of the nature of error (<s>bhrama</s>). Regarding this subject, disputants speak in many ways. In the world, it cannot be said that all cognitions of everyone about everything are valid (<s>pramā</s>). For if so, the opponent's cognition too would be valid, and thus the opponent too would be victorious. Nor can it be said that all cognition is invalid. For if so, the proponent's cognition too would be invalid,

children.text:
tathā ca vādi
parājito bhavet/ tasmāt kiñcit jñānaṃ pramā kiñcit jñānamapramā
iti vibhāgaḥ sarvairabhyupagantavyaḥ/ tatra apramātmake jñāne anyasya
anyathābhānātmikāmanyathākhyātiṃ naiyāyikā jainā bhāṭṭāśca
urarīkurvanti/ anyathākhyāteḥ yā sāmagrī bhedājñānarūpa akhyātiḥ tathaiva
vyavahāropapatteḥ akhyātipakṣa eva yukta iti prābhākarāḥ/
kṣaṇikavijñānarūpaḥ ātmaiva bāhyavastvākāreṇa pratīyata
ityātmakhyātivādinaḥ/ bauddhāḥ/ bhramasthale asadeva pratīyata iti
asatkhyātivādinaḥ mādhyamikāḥ/ bhrame sadasadanirvañcanīyaṃ vastūtpadyate
pratīyate cetyadvaitinaḥ/ etanmate anirvacanīyakhyātiḥ/
children.translated_text: and thus the proponent would be defeated. Therefore, the distinction that some cognition is valid and some cognition is invalid must be accepted by all. Among these, regarding cognition that is of the nature of invalidity, the <s>Naiyāyikas</s>, <s>Jainas</s>, and <s>Bhāṭṭas</s> accept <s>anyathākhyāti</s> (error as the apprehension of one thing as another). The <s>Prābhākaras</s> hold that the <s>akhyāti</s> view (error as mere non-apprehension of difference) alone is correct, since the causal aggregate of <s>anyathākhyāti</s> — namely non-apprehension of difference — is itself sufficient to explain practical behavior. The Buddhists hold <s>ātmakhyāti</s> (error as self-manifestation) — that the self, which is of the nature of momentary consciousness (<s>kṣaṇikavijñāna</s>), is apprehended in the form of external objects. The <s>Mādhyamikas</s> are proponents of <s>asatkhyāti</s> (error as apprehension of the non-existent) — that in the locus of error, what is absolutely non-existent is apprehended. The <s>Advaitins</s> hold that in error, an entity that is neither real nor unreal and indeterminable (<s>anirvacanīya</s>) is produced and apprehended. In their view, this is <s>anirvacanīyakhyāti</s> (the theory of indeterminable error).

children.text:

anyathākhyātivādina iti prasiddhiḥ/ nyāyadarśane prathamasūtreṇa

anātmanyātmeti duḥkhe sukhamiti' ityādi bhāṣamāṇaḥ vātsyāyanaḥ

tātparyadīkāyām1---
children.translated_text: Among these, the <s>Naiyāyikas</s> are well known as proponents of <s>anyathākhyāti</s>. In the <s>Nyāya</s> philosophy, having stated in the first <s>sūtra</s> that the highest good (<s>niḥśreyasa</s>) is attained from the knowledge of reality, it is established by the second <s>sūtra</s> beginning with 'suffering, birth...' that false knowledge (<s>mithyājñāna</s>) is indirectly the cause of <s>saṃsāra</s>. Therein, <s>Vātsyāyana</s>, while commenting 'false knowledge is of many kinds — regarding the self: that it does not exist, or that the non-self is the self, or that suffering is happiness,' and so on, considers that cognition of the form 'that in what is not that' is false knowledge. The <s>Vārttika</s> author too states: 'What then is this error? It is the cognition of that in what is not that.' The designation <s>anyathākhyāti</s> for this error, however, is of later origin. In the <s>Tātparyadīkā</s> —

'saṃprati saṃdihāno
viparyayasvarūpaṃ pṛcchati

anyathākhyātiṃ tu
vṛddhāḥ/'

children.translated_text: From this statement, it is known that the <s>anyathākhyāti</s> view belongs to the <s>Naiyāyikas</s>.
