children.translated_text: Here is the conclusion: First, from the contact of the sense organ with the nacre (<s>śukti</s>), a cognition of the form 'this is white and shining' arises; then, from awakened impressions (<s>saṃskāra</s>), there is a memory of silver; the non-apprehension of the difference between the object present before one and silver — up to this point, the <s>akhyāti</s> and <s>anyathākhyāti</s> proponents

children.text:
samānam/ tataḥ 'idaṃ
rajatam' ityākārakaṃ rajatatvābhāvavadviśeṣyakarajatatvaprakārakaṃ
viśiṣṭajñānamutpadyate, tata eva pravṛttiriti naiyāyikāḥ
tādṛśaviśiṣṭajñānakāraṇatvenābhimatābhyāṃ bhedāgrahasahitābhyāṃ
children.translated_text: is the same. From that, a qualified cognition arises having the form 'this is silver,' having as its qualificand what possesses the absence of silver-ness, and having silver-ness as its qualifier-mode. From that very [cognition] arises activity — thus the <s>Naiyāyikas</s>. [The qualified cognition arises] from the two [cognitions] accepted as the cause of such qualified cognition, namely the perception of the object before one accompanied by non-apprehension of difference, and the memory of silver —

children.text:
purovartivastupratyakṣarajatasmaraṇābhyāmeva pravṛttyādinirvāhe
madhye viśiṣṭajñānamanāvaśyakamiti prābhākarāḥ iti/
children.translated_text: since activity and the rest can be explained by the perception of the object before one and the memory of silver alone, a qualified cognition in between is unnecessary — thus the <s>Prābhākaras</s>.

children.text: viśiṣṭajñānasyāvaśyakatā
children.translated_text: The necessity of qualified cognition

children.text:
satyasthale pravṛtiṃ
prati viśiṣṭajñānasya hetutvāt asatyasthale 'pi viśiṣṭajñānameva
pravartakaṃ vācyam/ tathā ca
children.translated_text: Since in the case of a veridical situation, qualified cognition is the cause of activity, even in the case of an erroneous situation, it must be said that qualified cognition alone is the impeller [of activity]. And accordingly,

children.text:
'visaṃvādipravṛttiḥ
viśiṣṭajñānajanyā pravṛttitvāt satyapravṛttivat'
ityanumānamanyathākhyātau pramāṇam/ tathā
'rajatecchājanyaśuktiviṣayakapravṛttijanakarajatatvaprakārakaṃ jñānaṃ
śuktiviśeṣyakaṃ śuktipravṛttiprayojakajñānatvāt śuktau
śuktyarthapravṛttiprayojakajñānavat' ityādīnyanumānānyapi
anyathākhyātisādhakatayā maṇāvupanyastāni/
evamanuvyavasāyātmakapratyakṣamapyanyathākhyātau mānam/ tathā hi - śuktau
idaṃ rajatamiti bhramānantaram idaṃ rajatatayā jānāmi
ityanuvyavasāyo jāyate/
idaṃviśeṣyakarajatatvaprakārakajñānavāhanam iti hi tadarthaḥ/ tatra
vyavasāyasya idaṃviśeṣyakarajatatvaprakārakatvābhāve uktānuvyavasāyaḥ
kathaṃ ghaṭeta? jñānadvayapakṣe 'idaṃ jānāmi' 'rajataṃ jānāmi'
ityākārako hyanuvyavasāyaḥ syāt, na tu idaṃ rajataṃ jānāmi
iti/
children.translated_text: the inference 'Contradicted activity is produced by qualified cognition, because it is activity, like veridical activity' is the proof for <s>anyathākhyāti</s> (the theory of erroneous apprehension as "otherwise"). Similarly, inferences such as 'The cognition that has silver-ness as its qualifier-mode, that generates activity toward a shell having a desire for silver as its object, has the shell as its qualificand — because it is a cognition that prompts activity toward the shell for its own purpose, like [the cognition] in the case of a genuine shell' — these and other inferences too have been presented in the <s>Maṇi</s> (Tattvacintāmaṇi) as establishing <s>anyathākhyāti</s>. Thus, the introspective perception (<s>anuvyavasāya</s>) too serves as a means of proof for <s>anyathākhyāti</s>. For after the error 'this is silver' regarding a shell, the introspective cognition arises: 'I cognize this as silver.' Its meaning is: it conveys a cognition having 'this' as qualificand and silver-ness as qualifier-mode. If the [original] cognition lacked the character of having 'this' as qualificand and silver-ness as qualifier-mode, how could the said introspective cognition be coherent? On the hypothesis of two [separate] cognitions, the introspective cognition would have the form 'I cognize this' and 'I cognize silver' — but not 'I cognize this as silver.'

children.text: anyathākhyātiśabdārthavicāraḥ
children.translated_text: Investigation of the meaning of the term <s>anyathākhyāti</s>

children.text:
anyatraiva satā
ākāreṇa purovartino viśiṣṭatājñānamanyathākhyātiḥ/ anyatraiva sattvaṃ
tu pravṛttivādhasahakṛtāt nāstīti bādhakapratyayānniścīyate/ ato
bhrāntijñānabādhitasya satyarajatasyātrāsattvamāpādayituṃ na śakyate,
praṃvṛttibādhavirahāt/ na vā mantrādipratibaddhasyāgneḥ
sphoṭajananādipravattibādhāt mithyātvaniścayaprasaṅgaḥ/ tatra nāstīti
bādhakapratyayasyābhāvāt/
children.translated_text: <s>Anyathākhyāti</s> (erroneous apprehension) is a qualified cognition of the object before one with a form that exists elsewhere only. That it exists elsewhere only is ascertained from the sublating cognition 'it is not [silver],' assisted by the frustration of activity. Therefore, since real silver, sublated by the erroneous cognition, cannot be rendered non-existent here — due to the absence of frustration of activity [with respect to it]. Nor is there the consequence that fire, obstructed by mantras and the like, would be concluded to be unreal because its activity of producing bursting and the like is frustrated — because there the sublating cognition 'it is not' is absent.

children.text:
khyātyantaravādibhirapyantato gatvā
anyathākhyātiravaśyāśrayaṇīyā/ tathā hi---asatkhyātimate kimasat
asaditi pratīyate saditi vā? asaditi cet bhramatvāsaṃbhavaḥ/ asataḥ
asattvena bhānasya pramātvāt bādhapravṛttī ca na ghaṭetām/ saditi
pratīyate cet, asataḥ sattvena bhānāt anyathākhyātireva syāt/
ātmakhyātipakṣe ātmaśabditaṃ jñānaṃ kiṃ jñānamiti pratīyate? utārthaṃ
iti? ādyena bhramatvabādhapravṛttīnāmasaṃbhavaḥ/ dvitīye jñānasyārthātmanā
bhānādanyathākhyātireva svīkṛtā syāt/
children.translated_text: Even the proponents of other theories of error must ultimately resort to <s>anyathākhyāti</s>. For consider: on the <s>asatkhyāti</s> view (cognition of the non-existent), is the non-existent cognized as non-existent or as existent? If as non-existent, then erroneous character is impossible — because the appearance of the non-existent as non-existent is veridical, and sublation and [corrective] activity would not occur. If it is cognized as existent, then since the non-existent appears as existent, it would be <s>anyathākhyāti</s> itself. On the <s>ātmakhyāti</s> (self-cognition) view, is the cognition called 'self' cognized as cognition, or as an object? By the first option, erroneous character, sublation, and [corrective] activity would be impossible. In the second case, since cognition appears in the form of an object, <s>anyathākhyāti</s> itself would be accepted.

children.text:
prābhākaramate 'pi
grahaṇasmaraṇātmakajñānadvayāṅgīkārāt tat jñānadvayaṃ kiṃ
jñānadvayamiti pratīyate kiṃ vā ekatvena? ādye bādhapravṛttyorasaṃbhavaḥ/
dvitīye dvayasyaikatvena bhānāt anyathākhyātiḥ/
children.translated_text: On the <s>Prābhākara</s> view also, since two cognitions in the form of apprehension and memory are accepted, are those two cognitions cognized as two or as one? In the first case, sublation and [corrective] activity would be impossible. In the second case, since two appear as one, it is <s>anyathākhyāti</s>.

children.text:
jñānamasti viṣayo
nāstīti pakṣe viṣayaḥ kimavidyamānatvena pratīyate uta vidyamānatvena?
ādye pravṛttyādyasaṃbhavaḥ/ na jātu kaścit avidyamānatvena pratīte vastuni
pravartate/ dvitīye avidyamānasya vidyamānatvena bhānādanyathākhyātiḥ
iti/
children.translated_text: On the view that 'cognition exists but the object does not' — is the object cognized as non-existent or as existent? In the first case, activity and the rest would be impossible. No one ever acts toward an object cognized as non-existent. In the second case, since the non-existent appears as existent, it is <s>anyathākhyāti</s>.

children.text: ( 14 ) abhāvavicāraḥ
children.translated_text: ( 14 ) Investigation of <s>Abhāva</s> (Absence)

children.text:
tarkasaṃgrahe
dīpikāyāṃ ca abhāvasya caturdhā vibhāgaḥ atiriktapadārthatvaṃ ca
prādarśiṣātām/ idaṃ kiñcidvicāryate/
children.translated_text: In the <s>Tarkasaṃgraha</s> and the <s>Dīpikā</s>, the fourfold division of <s>abhāva</s> (absence) and its status as a separate category have been demonstrated. This is now briefly examined.

children.text:
'prāgutpatterabhāvopapatteśce' (nyā.sū.2-2-12) iti sūtre
bhāṣyam ---
children.translated_text: On the <s>sūtra</s> 'Because of the absence prior to origination and of destruction' (<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.2.12), the <s>Bhāṣya</s> states —

children.text:
'abhāvadvaitaṃ khalu
bhavati prāk cotpatteravidyamānatā
children.translated_text: 'Absence is indeed twofold: the non-existence prior to origination,

children.text:
utpannasya cātmano
hānādavidyamānatā'
children.translated_text: and the non-existence due to the destruction of what has come into being.'

children.text:
iti/
vārtikepyevameva pratipādyate/ tena prāgabhāvaḥ pradhvaṃsaśceti dvividha
evābhāvo bhāṣyavārttikakārayoḥ saṃmata iti pratīyate/ tatraiva
tātparyaṭīkākāraḥ ---
children.translated_text: Thus. In the <s>Vārtika</s> too, the same is set forth. Hence it appears that only a twofold absence — <s>prāgabhāva</s> (prior absence) and <s>pradhvaṃsa</s> (destruction) — is accepted by the authors of the <s>Bhāṣya</s> and <s>Vārtika</s>. There, the author of the <s>Tātparyaṭīkā</s> [says] —

children.text:
'abhāvadvaitamiti
prakṛtāpekṣam/ prakṛtaṃ pradhvaṃsamātra-
children.translated_text: '"Absence is twofold" — this is said with reference to the context. In relation to the one who holds only destruction [as absence],

children.text:
vādinaṃ prati
prāgabhāvapratipādanam/ paramārthatastu
children.translated_text: this is a demonstration of <s>prāgabhāva</s> (prior absence). But in the ultimate sense,

children.text:
prathamamabhāve
dvaitam--tādātmyābhāvaḥ saṃsargā-
children.translated_text: there is first a twofold division of absence — <s>tādātmyābhāva</s> (absence of identity, i.e. mutual absence) and <s>saṃsargābhāva</s> (relational absence).

children.text:
bhāvaśceti/
saṃsargābhāvo 'pi prākpradhvaṃsātyantābhāvena
children.translated_text: And <s>saṃsargābhāva</s> is threefold — as <s>prāk</s> (prior), <s>pradhvaṃsa</s> (destructional), and <s>atyantābhāva</s> (absolute absence).

children.text:
trividha iti catasro
vidhā abhāvasya'
children.translated_text: Thus the four varieties of absence.'

children.text:
ityabhāvacatuṣṭayamapi nyāyadarśanasaṃmatamiti pratyapādayat/
bhāvavadabhāvo 'pi pramāṇavedyaḥ/ yat pramāṇaṃ bhāvaṃ jñāpayati tadeva
pramāṇaṃ pratiyogyanupalabdhisahakṛtamabhāvaṃ jñāpayati ityāśayavāta
bhāṣyakāreṇa ---
children.translated_text: Thus he established that the fourfold classification of absence is accepted by the <s>Nyāya</s> system. Like positive entities, absence too is cognizable by valid means of knowledge. The means of knowledge that reveals a positive entity, assisted by the non-apprehension of the counter-positive, also reveals absence — with this intent, the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> [states] —

children.text:
'kathaṃ punaruttarasya
pramāṇenopalabdhiḥ/
children.translated_text: 'But how is the latter cognized by a means of knowledge?

children.text:
satyupalabhyamāne
tadvadanupalabdheḥ pradīpavat/
children.translated_text: When what is being apprehended is present, [the means of knowledge reveals it]; through the non-apprehension of what is like that — like a lamp.

children.text:
tadevaṃ sataḥ prakāśakaṃ
pramāṇamasadapi prakāśayati/'
children.translated_text: Thus the means of knowledge that illuminates the existent also illuminates the non-existent.'

children.text:
iti
prathamasūtre 'bhāṣi/ tatrābhāvasyāpi pramāṇasiddhatve tasya bhāvavat
upadeśaḥ kuto na kṛtaḥ ityāśaṅkāyāmāha vārtikakāraḥ ---
children.translated_text: Thus it was stated in the <s>Bhāṣya</s> on the first <s>sūtra</s>. When the question arises — if absence too is established by valid means of knowledge, why was it not separately taught like positive entities? — the <s>Vārtikakāra</s> answers —

children.text:
'sat khalu
pramāṇasyālambanaṃ svatantraṃ bhavati/
children.translated_text: 'The existent, indeed, serves as the independent object of a means of knowledge.

children.text:
asattu paratantraṃ
pratiṣedhamukhena pratipadyate/'
children.translated_text: But the non-existent, being dependent, is apprehended through the mode of negation.'

children.text:
iti niṣedhyaṃ
niṣedhādhikaraṇam ityubhayajñānādhīnatvāt abhāvasya, bhāve jñāte
abhāvo 'pi jñātaprāya ityāśayena sūtrakṛtā abhāvo na nirdiṣṭa
iti tadāśayaḥ/
children.translated_text: Since absence depends upon the knowledge of both what is negated and the locus of negation, when a positive entity is known, absence too is virtually known — with this intent, the <s>Sūtrakāra</s> did not separately mention absence. That is the purport.

children.text:
vaiśeṣikasūtreṣvapi
abhāvacatuṣṭayābhyupagamaḥ sūcito vartate/
'kriyāguṇavyapadeśābhāvāt prāgasat' (vai.sū.9-1-1)
children.translated_text: In the <s>Vaiśeṣikasūtras</s> also, the acceptance of the fourfold classification of absence is indicated. The <s>sūtra</s> 'Due to the absence of designation by action, quality [etc.], it is non-existent prior [to origination]' (<s>Vaiśeṣikasūtra</s> 9.1.1)

children.text:
iti sūtraṃ
ghaṭādirūpakāryasya utpatteḥ prāgavidyamānatāṃ pratipādayat
prāgabhāvamanumanyate/ utpatteḥ prāgavidyamānatā hi prāgabhāvo nāma/
tathā 'sadasat' (vai.sū.9-1-2) iti sūtraṃ sato ghaṭādeḥ
mudgarapātādyanantaramabhāvaṃ pratipādayat dhvaṃsākhyamabhāvaṃ sūcayati/
tataḥ 'saccāsat' (vai.sū.9-1-3) iti sūtraṃ satā ghaṭādeḥ paṭādyātmanā
abhāvaṃ bodhayatdhtt
children.translated_text: — this <s>sūtra</s>, by setting forth the non-existence of an effect such as a pot prior to its origination, implies <s>prāgabhāva</s> (prior absence). For the non-existence prior to origination is indeed what is called <s>prāgabhāva</s>. Similarly, the <s>sūtra</s> 'The existent [becomes] non-existent' (<s>Vaiśeṣikasūtra</s> 9.1.2), by teaching the absence of an existent thing like a pot after a blow from a mallet and the like, indicates the absence called <s>dhvaṃsa</s> (destruction). Then the <s>sūtra</s> 'The existent and the non-existent' (<s>Vaiśeṣikasūtra</s> 9.1.3), by conveying the absence of an existent pot in the form of a cloth and the like,

children.text:
tādātmyābhāvarūpamanyonyābhāvaṃ vyañjayati/ tataḥ
'yaccānyadasadatastadasat' (vai.sū.9-1-5) iti sūtram/ tatra
asacchabdadvayaṃ bhāvavapradhāno nirdeṃśaḥ/ yat ataḥ asataḥ anyat asat
tat asat ityanvayaḥ/ pūrvoktābhāvatrayāt anyo yo 'bhāvaḥ
so 'tyantābhāve iti/ evaṃ sthite abhāvasya pṛthaganupadeśaḥ
bhāvapāratantryāt na tvabhāvāditi sidhyati/
children.translated_text: suggests <s>anyonyābhāva</s> (mutual absence) in the form of absence of identity. Then the <s>sūtra</s> 'And that which is different from that non-existent is non-existent' (<s>Vaiśeṣikasūtra</s> 9.1.5). There, the two occurrences of the word 'non-existent' primarily refer to positive entities [i.e. absences as entities]. The construal is: that absence which is other than the aforementioned three types of absence is <s>atyantābhāva</s> (absolute absence). Being thus established, the separate non-enumeration of absence [in the <s>sūtra</s>] is justified by its dependence on positive entities, not by [any implication that] absence [is not a real category].

children.text: nyāyamañjarīkārāstu
children.translated_text: But the author of the <s>Nyāyamañjarī</s> —

children.text:
'na prāgabhāvādanye tu
bhidyante paramārthataḥ/
children.translated_text: 'No others besides <s>prāgabhāva</s> are ultimately distinct.

children.text:
sa hi
vastvantaropādhiranyonyābhāva ucyate//
children.translated_text: For that [absence], when conditioned by another entity, is called <s>anyonyābhāva</s> (mutual absence).

children.text:
sa
evāvadhiśūnyatvādatyantābhāvatāṃ gataḥ/
children.translated_text: That same [absence], being devoid of a terminus, attains the status of <s>atyantābhāva</s> (absolute absence).

children.text:
utpannasya vināśo vā
tadanutpāda eva vā/
children.translated_text: Or [it is] the destruction of what has arisen, or the very non-origination of that.

children.text:
abhāvastattvato 'nye tu
bhedāstvaupādhikā matāḥ//'1
children.translated_text: Absence is in reality [twofold]; but the other distinctions are considered to be based on limiting conditions.'

children.text:
iti granthena
prāgabhāvapradhvaṃsabhedenābhāvo dvividhaḥ/ anyonyātyantābhāvau
prāgabhāva evāntarbhavataḥ/ prāgabhāva eva vastvantarapratiyogikaścet
anyonyābhāva ityucyate/ sa evāvadhiśūnyaścet atyantābhāva iti
kathyate iti nyarūpayan/
children.translated_text: By this passage, [the <s>Nyāyamañjarīkāra</s>] explained that absence is twofold as <s>prāgabhāva</s> and <s>pradhvaṃsa</s>. <s>Anyonyābhāva</s> and <s>atyantābhāva</s> are subsumed under <s>prāgabhāva</s> itself. When <s>prāgabhāva</s> itself has a different entity as its counter-positive, it is called <s>anyonyābhāva</s>. When that same [absence] is devoid of a terminus, it is called <s>atyantābhāva</s> — thus he explained.

children.text:
prābhākārāḥ
atiriktamabhāvaṃ nāṅgīkurvanti/ abhāvaḥ buddhiviśeṣasvarūpaḥ,
adhikaraṇasvarūpaḥ kālaviśeṣasvarūpaḥ iti pakṣatrayaṃ pradarśayanti/
etatpakṣatrayamapi maṇau vistareṇa dūṣitam, tadanusāreṇa muktāvalyāṃ
ca/ dīpikāyāṃ tvadhikaraṇātmakatvapakṣaḥ anūdya dūṣita iti viśeṣaḥ/
children.translated_text: The <s>Prābhākaras</s> do not accept absence as a separate category. They present three hypotheses: absence is the nature of a particular cognition, the nature of the locus, or the nature of a particular time. All three hypotheses have been refuted at length in the <s>Maṇi</s> (Tattvacintāmaṇi), and following that, in the <s>Muktāvalī</s> also. In the <s>Dīpikā</s>, however, the specific point is that the view of absence being identical with its locus was cited and refuted.

children.text:
atra vicāryate/
abhāvādhikaraṇako 'bhāvaḥ adhikaraṇībhūtābhāvasvarūpa iti naiyāyikā
api svīkurvanti/ tatra
children.translated_text: Here it is examined. Even the <s>Naiyāyikas</s> accept that an absence whose locus is [another] absence has the nature of that absence which has become the locus. In that regard,

children.text:
'ghaṭābhāve na paṭaḥ'
ityādhārādheyabhāvaḥ pratīyate/ sa cādhārādheyayorabhede 'pi
ādhāratāvacchedakayorghaṭābhāvatvapaṭābhāvatvayorbhedānniruhyate/ tathā
'bhūtale ghaṭābhāva' iti pratītirapi bhūtalatvaghaṭābhāvatvayorbhedāt
nirūḍhā bhaviṣyati/ ataḥ adhikaraṇātmakatvamevābhāvasyāstu/
children.translated_text: 'In the absence of a pot, there is no cloth' — this relation of container and contained is cognized. And even when the container and contained are non-different, this [relation] is established due to the difference between the delimiting properties of container-ness, namely pot-absence-ness and cloth-absence-ness. Similarly, the cognition 'On the ground, there is absence of a pot' will also be established due to the difference between ground-ness and pot-absence-ness. Therefore, let absence simply be identical with its locus.

children.text:
śabdābhāvasya
gṛhasvarūpasya gṛhatvena rūpeṇa śrotrendriyavedyatvābhāve 'pi
śabdābhāvatvena rūpeṇa tadvedyatvaṃ
children.translated_text: Sound-absence, being the nature of the house, though it lacks cognizability by the auditory sense in its form as house-ness,

children.text:
bhaviṣyati/ yathā
naiyāyikamate 'pi rūpābhāvādhikaraṇakarasābhāvasya
rūpābhāvātmakatve 'pi rūpābhāvatvenaiva cākṣuṣaviṣayatā na
rasābhāvatvenetyaṅgīkriyate, tadvat/ tathā ca śabdādyabhāvānāṃ
pratyakṣatvānupapattirapi nāsti/
children.translated_text: will be cognizable by that [auditory sense] in its form as sound-absence-ness. Just as on the <s>Naiyāyika</s> view too, taste-absence whose locus is color-absence, even though identical with color-absence, is accepted as a visual object only in its form as color-absence-ness and not in its form as taste-absence-ness — so likewise. And thus there is no difficulty regarding the perceptibility of sound-absence and the like.

children.text:
tathā jñānaviśeṣatvena
kālaviśeṣatvena cāpratyakṣatve 'pi tattadabhāvatvena
jñānaviśeṣakālaviśeṣayoḥ pratyakṣatā saṃbhavatyeva/
ato 'bhāvasyānatiriktatve 'pi na ko 'pi doṣa iti/
children.translated_text: Similarly, even though a particular cognition and a particular time may not be perceptible in their form as such, they may be perceptible in their respective forms as particular absences. Therefore, even if absence is not a separate category, there is no defect.

children.text:
atra samādhīyate/
prāyaśo loke bhinnayorevādhārādheyabhāvaḥ prasiddhaḥ/ sa
cābhāvātiriktatvavādinaiyāyikamate sūpapādaḥ/
abhāvādhikaraṇakābhāvasthale
gatyantaravirahādādhārādheyabhāvapratītergauṇatayā nirvāhe 'pi
gatyantarasattve tathā nirvāhasyānucitatvāt/
ato 'dhikaraṇātmakatvapakṣo na yuktaḥ/
children.translated_text: Here is the resolution. Generally in the world, the relation of container and contained is well-known between entities that are distinct. That [relation] is easily explained on the <s>Naiyāyika</s> view that absence is a separate entity. In the case where absence is identical with its locus, although the cognition of the container-contained relation can be explained away as figurative due to the absence of any alternative, when an alternative exists, such an explanation would be inappropriate. Therefore the view that absence is identical with its locus is not justified.

children.text:
jñānaviśeṣarūpatvapakṣe
kālaviśeṣarūpatvapakṣe ca śabdādyabhāvānāṃ pratyakṣatvānupapattidoṣo
duruddharaḥ/ tatra yaduktaṃ jñānatvena kālatvena ca rūpeṇa
tayorbahirindriyagrāhyatvābhāve 'pi śabdādyabhāvatvena tattvamakṣatamiti,
tatrocyate/ rūpāntareṇāpi tayoḥ tādṛśapratyakṣaviṣayatvaṃ na saṃbhavati/
tathā hi gehe śabdo nāstīti pratītau śabdābhāvatvena rūpeṇa kiṃ
svātmakajñānaṃ viṣayaḥ? puruṣāntarīyajñānaṃ vā? nādyaḥ, pratyakṣe viṣayasya
kāraṇakatvāt pūrvakṣaṇe svātmakajñānasyābhāvāt pūrvakṣaṇe 'sataḥ
kāraṇatvāsaṃbhavāt/ na dvitīyaḥ, ekasmin abhāvajñāne bhūyasīnāṃ
puruṣāntarīyajñānavyaktīnāṃ viṣayatvakalpane gauravāt/ evaṃ
kālaviśeṣasyāpi na tādṛśapratyakṣaviṣayatvaṃ saṃbhavati,
tādṛśajñānotpattikṣaṇātmakakālasya pūrvapṛttitvābhāvāt/
pūrvakṣaṇātmakakālasya ca tatkāle 'bhāvāt/ na ca
jñānotpattikṣaṇatatpūrvakṣaṇobhayāvasthāyisthūlakālasya 'gehe śabdo
nāsti' ityādipratyakṣaviṣayatvamastu, tathā ca noktadoṣa iti
vācyam/ tathāpi tādṛśakṣaṇadvayāvasthāyinānāpadārtharūpasthūlakālasya
ekaikatādṛśajñānaviṣayatvakalpane gauravāditi nirūpayāmāsuḥ
muktāvalīmañjūṣākārāḥ/
children.translated_text: On the view that absence has the nature of a particular cognition, and on the view that it has the nature of a particular time, the defect of the impossibility of the perceptibility of sound-absence and the like is insurmountable. The claim made there — that though [cognition and time] are not graspable by external sense-organs in their form as cognition-ness and time-ness, they are perceptible in their form as sound-absence-ness and the like — to that we reply: even in another form, their being objects of such perception is not possible. For in the cognition 'There is no sound in the house' — what is the object in the form of sound-absence-ness? Is it a cognition identical with oneself? Or a cognition belonging to another person? Not the first, because in perception the object must be a cause, and a cognition identical with oneself at the prior moment is absent, and what is absent at the prior moment cannot be a cause. Nor the second, because it would be gratuitously complex to posit the many instances of other persons' cognitions as the object of a single cognition of absence. Similarly, a particular time too cannot be such a perceptual object, because the time consisting of the moment of the arising of such cognition does not have prior existence. And the time consisting of the prior moment is absent at that time. Nor should it be said: let a gross time persisting through both the moment of the cognition's arising and the prior moment be the perceptual object of 'there is no sound in the house' and the like, and thus the stated defect does not arise — for even so, the authors of the <s>Muktāvalīmañjūṣā</s> have shown that the gratuitous complexity of postulating a gross time consisting of different moments, each being many different entities, as the object of each such cognition [remains a defect].

children.text: ākhyātārthavicāraḥ śabdabodhaprakriyā ca
children.translated_text: Investigation of the meaning of verbal endings (<s>ākhyāta</s>) and the process of verbal cognition (<s>śabdabodha</s>)

children.text:
dīpikāyāṃ
prakāśikāyāṃ ca vidhyarthanirūpaṇaprasaṅgena ākhyātasya kṛtyarthakatvaṃ
prasādhya devadattaḥ taṇḍulaṃ pacatīti vākyasya
taṇḍulakarmakapākānukūlakṛtimān devadatta ityartha iti
nirūpitam/ etattatvaṃ kiñcidvicāryate/
children.translated_text: In the <s>Dīpikā</s> and the <s>Prakāśikā</s>, in the context of determining the meaning of injunctive [sentences], having established that the finite verb (<s>ākhyāta</s>) denotes the sense of <s>kṛti</s> (effort/activity), the sentence '<s>Devadatta</s> cooks rice' was analyzed as meaning '<s>Devadatta</s> possesses effort conducive to cooking whose object is rice.' This truth is now examined a little further.

children.text:
śābdabodho nāma
śabdajanyaṃ jñānam/ śabdo nāma
parasparānvitārthaṃpratipādakapadasamūhātmakaṃ vākyam/ padasamūho
vākyaṃ ityetāvanmātroktau 'gauraśvaḥ puruṣo hastī' ityādeḥ
ananvitārthakapadasamūhasyāpi vākyatvaṃ syāt/ ataḥ
parasparānvitārthaketyuktam/ gaurgacchati, aśvodhāvati ityanayoḥ
pratyekaṃ vākyatve 'pi tayordvayormilitvā ekavākyatvaṃ na bhavati,
dvayorvākyārthayoḥ parasparamananvayāt/ tasmāt sākṣādvā paraṃparayā
vā svārthaviśeṣaṇībhūtārthapratipādakayāvatpadaviśiṣṭaṃ
viśeṣyabhūtārthapratipādakaṃ padamekavākyamiti paryaṃvasyati/ idameva
'athaikatvā dekaṃ vākyaṃ sākāṅkṣa cedvibhāge syāt' iti
pūrvamīmāṃsāsūtre [3-1-46] uktam/ ekasminnarthe anyeṣāṃ
viśeṣaṇatayānvayaḥ iti sūcanāyaiva 'sākāṅkṣaṃ cedvibhāge syāt'
ityuktam/
children.translated_text: Verbal cognition (<s>śābdabodha</s>) is knowledge born from words. A word (<s>śabda</s>) is a sentence (<s>vākya</s>) consisting of a collection of words that convey mutually connected meanings. If one were to say merely 'a collection of words is a sentence,' then even a collection of words conveying unconnected meanings such as 'cow, horse, man, elephant' would have sentence-hood. Therefore it is said 'conveying mutually connected meanings.' Even though 'the cow goes' and 'the horse runs' each individually have sentence-hood, the two together do not form a single sentence, because the meanings of the two sentences are not mutually connected. Therefore, the definition ultimately amounts to this: a single sentence is the qualifier-denoting word together with every word that denotes a meaning that becomes a qualifier of its own meaning — either directly or indirectly — along with the qualificand-denoting word. This very [definition] has been stated in the <s>Pūrvamīmāṃsāsūtra</s> [3.1.46]: 'When there is unity, it is one sentence; if there is expectancy, there would be division.' The statement 'if there is expectancy, there would be division' is made precisely to indicate that in one meaning, the connection of the others is as qualifiers.

children.text:
tatra padeṣu bahuṣu
prayujyamāneṣu kasya padārthasya kiṃ viśeṣaṇam? kiṃ
kimavāntaraviśeṣyam? kiṃ mukhyaviśeṣyamiti vicāraṇīyaṃ bhavati/
tatra vaiyākaraṇāḥ mīmāṃsakāḥ naiyāyikāśca bhinnabhinnaṃ
panthānamāśrayante/
children.translated_text: There, when many words are employed, one must consider: of which word-meaning is what the qualifier? What is what subordinate qualificand? What is the chief qualificand? In this regard, the grammarians (<s>Vaiyākaraṇas</s>), the <s>Mīmāṃsakas</s>, and the logicians (<s>Naiyāyikas</s>) each follow different paths.

children.text: vaiyākaraṇamatam
children.translated_text: The grammarians' view

children.text:
tathā hi
vaiyākaraṇāstāvadevaṃ manyante --- kārakāṇāṃ kriyāyāmanvayaḥ
ityanubhavāt kriyāpade prāyaḥ subantānāmanvaya iti pratīyate/
nīlotpalamānayatītyatra samāsārthasya nīlatvaviśiṣṭotpalasya
dvitīyārthe karmaṇi tasya dhātvarthe ānayane 'nvaya iti
nīlatvaviśiṣṭotpalakarmakamānayanamiti bodho bhavati/
nīlamutpalamānayeti vyāsasthale 'pi nīlakarmakamānayanam
utpalakarmakānayanamiti pṛthak pṛthak bodhasyānanubhavāt dviḥ
karmatvabhānaṃ vihāya samānādhikaraṇayornīlotpalapadayoḥ
nīlatvaviśiṣṭotpalarūpaikārthaparatvamaṅgīkṛtya tasya dhātvarthe
ānayane dvitīyārthakarmatvadvārā anvayasvīkārāt
nīlatvaviśiṣṭotpalakarmakamānayanamityeva bodhaḥ/ evaṃ ca
saviśeṣaṇānāṃ viśeṣaṇarahitānāṃ vā kartratiriktānāṃ sarveṣāṃ
kārakāṇāṃ dhātvarthakriyānvayasya naiyāyikādibhirapi svīkṛtatvāt
prathamāntārthasya kartṛkārakasyāpi tathaivānvaya ucitaḥ, samānanyāyāt/
tathā ca devadattaḥ nīlotpalamānayatītyatra ditīyārthaḥ karma, tatra
prakṛtyarthasya nīlatvaviśiṣṭotpalasyābhedasaṃbandhenānvayaḥ/ karmaṃṇaḥ
dhātvarthe 'nvayaḥ/ tiṅaḥ kartā arthaḥ/ tatrābhedasaṃbandhena
prathamāntapadārthasya devadattasyānvayaḥ/ kartuṃrapi dhātvarthe
ānayana'nvayaḥ/ tathā ca
children.translated_text: Thus, the grammarians hold as follows — since it is experienced that the <s>kārakas</s> (case-relations) are connected with the action, it is understood that the <s>subanta</s> (nominal) words generally connect with the action-word. In '<s>nīlotpalam ānayati</s>' (he brings a blue lotus), the compound meaning — blue-qualified lotus — connects through the second case meaning of objecthood with the verbal root meaning of bringing; thus the cognition is 'bringing whose object is a lotus qualified by blueness.' Even in the expanded form '<s>nīlam utpalam ānaya</s>' (bring the blue lotus), since we do not experience separate cognitions such as 'bringing whose object is blueness' and 'bringing whose object is a lotus' — setting aside the appearance of double objecthood, by accepting that the co-referential words <s>nīla</s> and <s>utpala</s> denote a single meaning in the form of 'lotus qualified by blueness,' and accepting its connection with the verbal root meaning of bringing through the objecthood that is the meaning of the second case — the cognition is precisely 'bringing whose object is a lotus qualified by blueness.' And thus, since the connection of all <s>kārakas</s> other than the agent — whether with qualifiers or without qualifiers — with the action denoted by the verbal root is accepted even by the <s>Naiyāyikas</s> and others, the connection of the agent <s>kāraka</s> too, which is the meaning of the nominative case, should be the same, by parity of reasoning. Accordingly, in '<s>Devadattaḥ nīlotpalam ānayati</s>' (<s>Devadatta</s> brings a blue lotus), the second case meaning is objecthood; therein the connection of the stem-meaning 'lotus qualified by blueness' is through the relation of identity. The object connects with the verbal root meaning. The meaning of the personal ending (<s>tiṅ</s>) is the agent. Therein the connection of the first-case word-meaning <s>Devadatta</s> is through the relation of identity. The agent too connects with the verbal root meaning of bringing. And thus,

children.text:
nīlatvaviśiṣṭotpalābhinnakarmakaṃ devadattābhinnakartṛkaṃ
cānayanamiti dhātvarthamukhyaviśeṣyako bodhaḥ/ atra pramāṇaṃ tu
'bhāvapradhānamākhyātam' iti niruktavacanaṃ 'kriyāpradhānamākhyātam'
iti mahābhāṣyavacanaṃ cetyāhuḥ/
children.translated_text: the cognition has the verbal root meaning as its chief qualificand: 'bringing whose object is identical with a lotus qualified by blueness and whose agent is identical with <s>Devadatta</s>.' The authority for this is the statement from the <s>Nirukta</s>: 'The finite verb (<s>ākhyāta</s>) has action as its principal element,' and the statement from the <s>Mahābhāṣya</s>: 'The finite verb has action as its principal element' — so they say.

children.text: mīmāṃsakamatam
children.translated_text: The <s>Mīmāṃsaka</s> view

children.text:
mīmāṃsakāstu --
tiṅarthabhāvanāmukhyaviśeṣyakaṃ bodhaṃ varṇayanti/ tathā hi
taṇḍulamityādīni dvitīyāntāni padāni kriyāpadaṃ vinā
nirākāṅkṣaṃ bodhaṃ na janayantītyanubhavasiddham/ tena tiṅantapadaṃ
viśeṣyasamarpakamiti labhyate/ tatrāpi 'prakṛtipratyayau pratyayārthaṃ saha
brūtastayostu pratyayaḥ prādhānyena' iti vyutpattibalāt
pratyayārthasyaiva prādhānyaṃ vaktavyamiti tiṅarthaḥ bhāvanāparaparyāyā
kṛtireva śābdabodhe mukhyaviśeṣyabhūtā/ 'evaṃ ca caitrastaṇḍulaṃ
pacati' iti vākye
children.translated_text: The <s>Mīmāṃsakas</s>, however, describe the cognition as having <s>bhāvanā</s> (productive activity), which is the meaning of the personal ending (<s>tiṅ</s>), as its chief qualificand. Thus: the second-case words such as '<s>taṇḍulam</s>' (rice) etc. do not generate a cognition free from expectancy without the action-word — this is established by experience. Therefore, the finite verb (<s>tiṅanta</s>) word is understood to present the qualificand. Therein also, by the force of the derivation 'the stem and the suffix together express the suffix's meaning, and of the two, the suffix has primacy,' the meaning of the suffix alone must be said to be primary; thus the meaning of the personal ending (<s>tiṅ</s>), namely <s>kṛti</s> (effort/activity) — which is synonymous with <s>bhāvanā</s> (productive activity) — alone is the chief qualificand in verbal cognition. And thus, in the sentence '<s>Caitraḥ taṇḍulaṃ pacati</s>' (<s>Caitra</s> cooks rice),

children.text:
dvitīyāyāḥ
karmatvamarthaḥ/ tatra taṇḍulasya ādheyatāsambandhenānvayaḥ/ karmatvasya
nirūpakatāsaṃbandhena (svanirūpakadhātvarthānukūlatvaparyavasitena)
tiṅarthakakṛtāvanvayaḥ/ dhātvarthasya pākasya
svakaraṇakaudanoddeśyakatvasambandhena kṛtāvanvayaḥ/
caitrapadottaraprathamāyāḥ prātipadikārthaḥ caitro 'thaḥ/ caitrapadaṃ
tātparyagrāhakam/ prathamārthasya caitrasya ādheyatāsaṃbandhena
bhāvanāyāmanvayaḥ/ ākhyātārthakālasaṃkhyayo 'pi bhāvanāyāmevānvayaḥ/
saṃkhyāyāḥ sāmānādhikaraṇyasambandhenānvayaḥ, kālasya
ādheyatāsaṃbandhenānvaya iti viśeṣa/ evaṃ ca caitraniṣṭhā
taṇḍulakarmakapākakaraṇakaudanoddeśyikā vartamānā ekā bhāvaneti
bodhaḥ/ 'bhāvapradhānamākhyātam' iti nirukte ākhyātaśabdaḥ tiṅparaḥ/
bhāvayatīti vyutpattyā ṇijantāt bhūdhātoracpratyayāntatvena niṣpannaḥ
bhāvaśabdaḥ bhāvanāvācī/ tiṅśca saṃkhyā kālaḥ bhāvanā iti
trayor'thāḥ/ teṣu bhāvanā pradhānabhūtā iti
bhāvanāmukhyaviśeṣyakabodhameva niruktakāro manyata iti
nirūpayanti/
children.translated_text: objecthood is the meaning of the second case. Therein, the connection of rice is through the relation of superstratum (<s>ādheyatā</s>). The connection of objecthood with the <s>kṛti</s> (effort) that is the meaning of the personal ending is through the relation of determinacy (<s>nirūpakatā</s>) — which amounts to being conducive to the verbal root meaning that is its own determinant. The connection of the verbal root meaning, cooking (<s>pāka</s>), with <s>kṛti</s> is through the relation of having that [cooking] as its instrument, with the boiled rice (<s>odana</s>) as its purpose. The meaning of the first case following the word '<s>Caitra</s>' is <s>Caitra</s> — the stem-meaning. The word '<s>Caitra</s>' is the indicator of purport (<s>tātparya</s>). The connection of <s>Caitra</s>, the first-case meaning, with <s>bhāvanā</s> is through the relation of superstratum. The tense and number that are the meanings of the finite verb also connect with <s>bhāvanā</s> alone. The connection of number is through the relation of co-referentiality (<s>sāmānādhikaraṇya</s>), while the connection of tense is through the relation of superstratum — this is the distinction. And thus the cognition is: '<s>bhāvanā</s> (productive activity) that belongs to <s>Caitra</s>, that is present [tense], that is singular, whose instrument is cooking that has rice as its object and boiled rice as its purpose.' In the <s>Nirukta</s>, the word '<s>ākhyāta</s>' (finite verb) refers to the personal ending (<s>tiṅ</s>). The word '<s>bhāva</s>,' derived from the causative form of the root <s>bhū</s> with the <s>ac</s> suffix, denotes <s>bhāvanā</s>. The personal ending (<s>tiṅ</s>) has three meanings: number, tense, and <s>bhāvanā</s>. Among these, <s>bhāvanā</s> is the principal one — thus the author of the <s>Nirukta</s> holds that the cognition has <s>bhāvanā</s> as its chief qualificand — so they explain.

children.text: naiyāyikamatam
children.translated_text: The <s>Naiyāyika</s> view

children.text:
'paṇḍitaścaitraḥ'
iti vākyam paṇḍitābhinnaścaitra iti bodho 'nubhūyate/ tatra
tiṅantapadābhāvāt dhātvarthasya vā tiṅarthabhāvanāyā vā
mukhyaviśeṣyatayā bhānaṃ na saṃbhavati/ tathā ca kvacit
prathamāntārthamukhyaviśeṣyakabodhasya svīkaraṇīyatayā
niṅntasamabhivyāhārasthalepi tathaiva bodhavarṇanaṃ yuktam/ na ca
tatrāpi yogyakriyādhyāhāreṇaiva śābdabodha iti vācyam/
anadhyāhāreṇaiva nirvāhe adhyāhārasyāyuktatvāt/ api ca
vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇe -- 'prāyaśo vākyasya suptiṅantasamudāyatvāt'
iti vadantaḥ kauṇḍabhaṭṭāḥ tiṅantaśūnyamapi vākyamabhyupagacchanti/
tathā ākhyātārthavyāpārāśrayatvarūpasya kartṛtvasya nirākaraṇāvasare
'ākhyātaśūnye devadattaḥ paktetyādau devadattasyākartṛtvāpatteḥ' iti
bhūṣaṇasāre 'pi tiṅantarahitavākyaprāmāṇyāṅgīkāraḥ pratīyate/ evaṃ
ca tiṅantāsamabhivyāhārasthale prathamāntārthaviśeṣyakabodhasya
svīkāryatvāt caitraḥ pacatītyādāvapi tathaiva bodhavarṇanaṃ yuktam/
tathā ca 'caitraḥ taṇḍulaṃ pacati' iti vākye
taṇḍulapadottaradvitīyāyāḥ karmatvamarthaḥ/ karmatve prakṛtyarthasya
taṇḍulasyādheyatāsaṃbandhenānvayaḥ/ karmatvasya nirūpakatāsambandhena
dhātvarthe pāke 'nvayaḥ/ ākhyātārthaḥ kṛtiḥ/ tatrānukūlatāsaṃbandhena
dhātvarthapākasyānvayaḥ/ kṛteśca āśrayatāsaṃbandhena
prathamāntārthecaitre 'nvayaḥ/ ākhyātārthasya vartamānakālasya
kṛtāvevānvayaḥ/ ākhyātaikavacanasya tu naikatvasaṃkhyā arthaḥ/
subekavacanenaiva ekatvalābhāt/ tathā ca
taṇḍulaniṣṭhakarmatānirūpakapākānukūlavartamānakṛtimān
ekatvāśrayaścaitra ityanvayabodhaḥ/
children.translated_text: In the sentence '<s>paṇḍitaś Caitraḥ</s>' (learned <s>Caitra</s>), the cognition experienced is '<s>Caitra</s> who is identical with a learned one.' There, due to the absence of a finite verb, neither the verbal root meaning nor <s>bhāvanā</s> which is the meaning of the personal ending can appear as the chief qualificand. And thus, since in some cases a cognition having the nominative-case meaning as chief qualificand must be accepted, it is proper to describe the cognition in the same way even where there is co-occurrence with a finite verb. Nor should it be said that even there, verbal cognition occurs only through supplying an appropriate action — for when explanation is possible without supplying, supplying is inappropriate. Moreover, in the <s>Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇa</s>, <s>Kauṇḍabhaṭṭa</s>, saying 'since a sentence is mostly a collection of nominal and verbal endings,' accepts even a sentence devoid of a finite verb. Similarly, in the <s>Bhūṣaṇasāra</s>, when refuting agent-hood as having the character of being the locus of the activity of the finite verb meaning, the statement 'in a finite-verb-less [sentence] like "<s>Devadattaḥ paktā</s>" (<s>Devadatta</s> is a cook), <s>Devadatta</s> would fail to be an agent' also indicates the acceptance of the validity of sentences without finite verbs. And thus, since cognition having the nominative-case meaning as qualificand must be accepted in contexts without co-occurrence of a finite verb, it is proper to describe the cognition in the same way even in '<s>Caitraḥ pacati</s>' (<s>Caitra</s> cooks) and the like. Accordingly, in the sentence '<s>Caitraḥ taṇḍulaṃ pacati</s>' (<s>Caitra</s> cooks rice): objecthood is the meaning of the second case following '<s>taṇḍula</s>.' In objecthood, the connection of the stem-meaning rice is through the relation of superstratum. The connection of objecthood with cooking (<s>pāka</s>), the verbal root meaning, is through the relation of determinacy. The meaning of the finite verb is <s>kṛti</s> (effort). Therein the connection of cooking, the verbal root meaning, is through the relation of being conducive to. And the connection of <s>kṛti</s> with the nominative-case meaning <s>Caitra</s> is through the relation of locus (<s>āśrayatā</s>). The present tense, which is the meaning of the finite verb, also connects with <s>kṛti</s> alone. The singular number of the finite verb, however, has non-plurality as its meaning — since singularity is already obtained from the singular nominal ending itself. And thus the verbal cognition is: '<s>Caitra</s>, who is the locus of present <s>kṛti</s> (effort) conducive to cooking determined by objecthood residing in rice, and who is the substratum of singularity.'

children.text:
kiṃ ca
'sarvanāmnāmutsargataḥ pradhānaparāmarśitvam' iti nyāyāt
pūrvavākyārthe yaḥ pradhānaḥ tasyaiva tacchabdena parāmarśo vaktavyaḥ/
dhātvarthamukhyaviśeṣyakasya ākhyātārthakṛtimukhyaviśeṣyakasya vā
bodhasyāṅgīkāre 'puruṣaḥ prayāti, tasya pādayorabhivādaya'
ityatrānupapattiḥ/ puruṣaḥ prayāti iti vākye pradhānasya gamanasya
kṛtervā tacchabdena parāmarśe
pādayorabhivādayetyanenānvayasyāsaṃgateḥ/ naiyāyikamate tu
puruṣasyaiva pradhānatayā tasya tacchabdena parāmarśeṃ
pādayorabhivādayetyanenānvayaḥ sādhuḥ saṃgataḥ/
children.translated_text: Furthermore, by the maxim that 'pronouns primarily refer to the principal element,' the pronoun 'that' (<s>tat</s>) should refer to what is principal in the meaning of the preceding sentence. If one accepts the cognition as having the verbal root meaning as chief qualificand, or <s>kṛti</s> (the meaning of the finite verb) as chief qualificand, then in the passage 'The man departs; salute his feet' — there would be incoherence. In the sentence 'the man departs,' if the pronoun 'his' (<s>tasya</s>) refers to going (the principal element) or to <s>kṛti</s>, the connection with 'salute the feet' would be incongruous. But on the <s>Naiyāyika</s> view, since the man himself is principal, the reference to him by the pronoun 'his' makes the connection with 'salute the feet' proper and coherent.

children.text:
kiṃ ca pratyakṣānubhave
yasya yena saṃbandhaḥ pratītasyasya tena saṃbandhaṃ tathaiva jñāpayituṃ vākyaṃ
prayujyate/ pratyakṣeṇa ca kārakāṇāṃ kriyānvaya evāvagamyate, na tu
kṛtyaparaparyāyabhāvanānvayaḥ/ ato mīmāṃsakamataṃ nocitam/ nāpi
vaiyākaraṇamatam/ pratyakṣe dharmasya prakāratāyāḥ dharmiṇo
kśiṣyatāyāścānubhavasiddhatayā dharmabhūtadhātvarthāpekṣayā dharmiṇaḥ
prathamāntārthaṃsyaiva viśeṣyatvaucityāt/ tatrāpi
prakṛtipratyayārthayormadhye pratyayārthasya pradhānatvāt tiṅvācyāyāḥ
kṛteḥ dhātvarthaṃ prati viśeṣyatvāt tādṛśakṛtyāśrayasya
devadattāderviśeṣyatvamucitam/ sakalakarmādikārakaprerakasya
kriyākartuḥ
children.translated_text: Furthermore, in perceptual experience, the sentence is used to convey the connection of something with something else exactly as it has been cognized. And by perception, only the connection of <s>kārakas</s> with action is apprehended, not the connection with <s>bhāvanā</s> (productive activity), which is synonymous with <s>kṛti</s>. Therefore the <s>Mīmāṃsaka</s> view is not appropriate. Nor is the grammarians' view — because in perception, since the qualifier-ness of the property and the qualificand-ness of the property-bearer are established by experience, in comparison with the verbal root meaning which is a property, it is appropriate that the nominative-case meaning, the property-bearer, be the qualificand. Therein also, among the stem-meaning and the suffix-meaning, since the suffix-meaning has primacy, and since <s>kṛti</s> denoted by the personal ending is the qualificand in relation to the verbal root meaning, it is appropriate that the locus of such <s>kṛti</s>, namely <s>Devadatta</s> and the like, be the qualificand. The primacy of the agent of the action, who impels all <s>kārakas</s> such as the object etc.,

children.text:
sarvāpekṣayā prādhānyaṃ
hi ānubhavikam/
children.translated_text: over all [other elements] is indeed a matter of experience.

children.text:
api ca pāṇiniḥ
'prātipadikārtha' ityādinā sūtreṇa prathamāyāḥ prātipadikārtha
evārtha iti vadan kārakārthakatvaṃ
children.translated_text: Moreover, <s>Pāṇini</s>, by the <s>sūtra</s> beginning with '<s>prātipadikārtha</s>' (the meaning of a nominal stem), stating that the meaning of the first case (<s>prathamā</s>) is only the stem-meaning, does not sanction

children.text:
nānumanyate/ tena ca
prathamāntārthasya kriyāyāmanvayaḥ tasyā nānumata iti spaṣṭam/
kārakārthakatve hi
children.translated_text: objecthood as [its] meaning. And thereby it is clear that the connection of the nominative-case meaning with action is not sanctioned by him. For if objecthood were [its] meaning,

children.text:
kriyānvayamūlakaḥ
kriyāpradhānakatvanirbandhaḥ/ tasmāt prathamāntārthaviśeṣyakabodha
evāsati bādhake ucitaḥ/ sati tu bādhake bhāvākhyātasthale caitreṇa
supyate ityādau, paśya mṛgo dhāvatītyādau ca
dhātvarthādimukhyaviśeṣyako 'pi bodhaḥ svīkriyate iti
naiyāyikasiddhāntasāraḥ/
children.translated_text: the insistence on action-principality would be based on connection with action. Therefore, cognition having the nominative-case meaning as qualificand alone is appropriate in the absence of a defeater. But in the presence of a defeater — in the case of impersonal verbs, as in '<s>Caitreṇa supyate</s>' (<s>Caitra</s> sleeps [lit. it is slept by <s>Caitra</s>]), and in cases like '<s>paśya mṛgo dhāvati</s>' (look, the deer runs) — cognition having the verbal root meaning etc. as chief qualificand is also accepted. This is the essence of the <s>Naiyāyika</s> position.

For the purpose of the unobstructed completion of the intended work, composing in the text an auspicious invocation (<s>maṅgala</s>) in the form of salutation to the chosen deity — which is a duty indicated by scripture inferred from the practice of the learned — for the instruction of the student, [the author] declares his intention:

children.translated_text: Objection: The auspicious invocation does not have the power to bring about completion. For even when the invocation is performed, non-completion is seen in cases like the <s>Kiraṇāvalī</s>; and even without the invocation, completion is seen in cases like the <s>Kādambarī</s>. Thus there is deviation established by both positive and negative concomitance. Reply: No.

Now, if asked what is the proof for the obligatory nature of the auspicious invocation (<s>maṅgala</s>) — no [separate proof is needed], because the <s>śruti</s> (Vedic scripture) inferred from the conduct of the learned is itself the authority. Thus: the auspicious invocation has an obligatoriness taught by the <s>Veda</s>, because it is the object of the conduct of the learned that is extraordinary and uncontested — like the <s>Darśa</s> sacrifice and the like. The qualifier 'extraordinary' is to prevent the counterexample of eating and the like. The qualifier 'uncontested' is to prevent the counterexample of nocturnal <s>śrāddha</s> and the like. The word 'learned' (<s>śiṣṭa</s>) is self-explanatory. Because of the prohibition 'One should not perform a fruitless action,' even striking water and the like are prohibited. <s>Tarkāḥ</s> — the things that are investigated, i.e. the categories (<s>padārthas</s>) such as substance (<s>dravya</s>) and the rest — their <s>saṅgraha</s> (compendium) — means their nature is stated in brief. For what purpose? To that he says —

vedabodhitakartavyatākatvarūpavakṣyamāṇavidheyakoṭipraviṣṭatve 'pi
tadantarbhāveṇa vidheyatvamabhyupagamyate/ tacchruteḥ anumiteḥ
pūrvamasiddhatvāt etena 'vahnyādisādhyakānumitiviṣayatāmādāya

ityanumānarūpapramāṇāntarasattve 'pi na kṣatiḥ/ anye tu
--'svabodhitakartavyatākatvasambandhena śrutereva sādhyatā/
agrimagranthasyātraiva tātparyam/ evaṃ ca śruteranumitatvopapattiḥ'
ityāhuḥ/
children.translated_text: that is. Here the intent is as follows: even though <s>śruti</s> enters the category of the predicate (<s>vidheya</s>) to be stated, namely having obligatoriness taught by the <s>Veda</s>, its predicatedness is accepted through its inclusion therein. Since that <s>śruti</s> is not established prior to the inference — by this, the objection 'how can the usage of inferred apply to <s>śruti</s>, since there is no usage like fire and the like are inferred taking the object-hood of inferences that establish things like fire' is refuted — because, having accepted the predicatedness of <s>śruti</s>, there is no invalidating factor for such usage. The particle '<s>eva</s>' (alone) is also meaningful. By this, even if there exists another means of knowledge in the form of inference such as 'the auspicious invocation ought to be performed because it brings about completion,' there is no harm. Others, however, say — 'The <s>śruti</s>'s being the thing to be proved is in relation to having obligatoriness taught by itself. The purport of the next passage is toward this alone. And thus the justification for <s>śruti</s> being called inferred is established.'
In order to establish that the obligatoriness of the auspicious invocation is taught by <s>śruti</s>, he raises a doubt — with 'now' (<s>nanu</s>) and so forth.

children.translated_text: The purport is as follows: the cause of the ascertainment of causality is the ascertainment of invariable positive co-occurrence and the ascertainment of invariable negative co-occurrence. Invariable positive co-occurrence means being an effect pervaded by the cause. Invariable negative co-occurrence means being an absence-of-effect pervaded by the absence of the cause. Deviation in positive concomitance means the absence of the effect even when the cause is present — that is, the effect not being pervaded by the cause. Deviation in negative concomitance means the presence of the effect even when the cause is absent — that is, the absence-of-effect not being pervaded by the absence of the cause. There, the knowledge of deviation in positive concomitance is an obstruction to the knowledge of invariable positive co-occurrence. The knowledge of deviation in negative concomitance is an obstruction to the knowledge of invariable negative co-occurrence. In the present case, even when the cause in the form of the auspicious invocation is present, since the effect in the form of completion is not seen in the case of <s>Kiraṇāvalī</s> and the like, the auspicious invocation

From the <s>Dīpikā</s> passage beginning with 'of what is intended,' it is obtained that the purpose of the auspicious invocation is the unobstructed completion, and the purpose of the treatise based upon it is the instruction of students. There, the causal relation between the auspicious invocation and the completion of the treatise is not possible, due to deviation in positive concomitance and deviation in negative concomitance — this was doubted in the <s>Dīpikā</s> with the passage 'Now, of the auspicious invocation.' Thus, even in the absence of a cause in the form of <s>maṅgala</s>, since the effect in the form of <s>samāpti</s> is observed in the <s>Kādambarī</s> and other works, the pervasion by the absence of <s>maṅgala</s> does not hold for the absence of <s>samāpti</s>, because <s>samāpti</s> exists even where the absence of <s>maṅgala</s> obtains. And accordingly, because there exists a hindrance in the form of the determination '<s>maṅgala</s> is such that its own absence is not pervaded by the absence of <s>samāpti</s>' — a determination of invariable negative concomitance of the form '<s>maṅgala</s> is that whose own absence is pervaded by the absence of <s>samāpti</s>' does not arise. And accordingly, due to the absence of the cause in the form of a determination of invariable positive and negative concomitance, a determination engaging the property of being a cause delimited by <s>samāpti</s> in <s>maṅgala</s> — that is, a determination of the form '<s>maṅgala</s> is the cause of <s>samāpti</s>' — does not arise.

children.translated_text: For <s>maṅgala</s> is not directly the cause of <s>samāpti</s> (completion), but rather through the medium of the destruction of obstacles. And the destruction of obstacles arises from a <s>maṅgala</s> that is fewer in number than the obstacles or more powerful [than them]. Accordingly, a <s>maṅgala</s> that is fewer in number than the obstacles or more powerful is the cause of <s>samāpti</s>. And in the <s>Kiraṇāvalī</s> and other works, because of the abundance of obstacles, such a <s>maṅgala</s> does not exist, and therefore the effect in the form of <s>samāpti</s> did not occur. Hence there is no deviation in positive concomitance in the form of the absence of the effect when the cause is present — this is the purport. If it had been said 'whose number is equal to the obstacles,' then the causality of a <s>maṅgala</s> whose number exceeds the obstacles would be desired but could not be established — therefore it was said —
